Diffusion-Based Sampling for Unnormalized Distributions

DATA8018 Group Blog · April 2026
Table of Contents ▼

1. The problem: data-free sampling

Suppose you have a formula that scores every possible configuration of a system: how likely each protein shape is, how good each solution to a scheduling problem is, how plausible each setting of model parameters is given observed data. You can plug in any configuration and get a number back. What you cannot easily do is generate configurations that score highly. That is the problem this post is about.

More precisely, we have an unnormalized density π(x)\pi(x)π(x) that we can evaluate pointwise, and we want to draw samples from the corresponding probability distribution:

p(x)=π(x)Z,Z=∫π(x) dxp(x) = \frac{\pi(x)}{Z}, \qquad Z = \int \pi(x)\,dxp(x)=Zπ(x)​,Z=∫π(x)dx

The catch is the normalizing constant ZZZ. It sums (or integrates) π\piπ over every possible configuration. In low dimensions this is tractable, but in the high-dimensional spaces that arise in practice, such as thousands of spins or hundreds of model parameters, computing ZZZ is hopelessly expensive. Without ZZZ we cannot evaluate p(x)p(x)p(x) directly, so methods that need normalized probabilities are usually off the table. We need algorithms that work with only the unnormalized π(x)\pi(x)π(x), or with ratios such as π(x′)/π(x)\pi(x')/\pi(x)π(x′)/π(x).

The target may live in continuous space (x∈Rdx \in \mathbb{R}^dx∈Rd) or discrete space (x∈{0,1}Nx \in \{0,1\}^Nx∈{0,1}N). A particularly common form is the Boltzmann distribution π(x)=e−βH(x)\pi(x) = e^{-\beta H(x)}π(x)=e−βH(x), where H(x)H(x)H(x) is an energy function that assigns a cost to each configuration and β\betaβ (inverse temperature) controls how sharply probability concentrates on low-energy states. At low β\betaβ the distribution is spread out; at high β\betaβ it collapses onto the global minima of HHH.

Figure 1. Boltzmann density for a double-well energy H(x)=(x2−4)2/40H(x) = (x^2-4)^2/40H(x)=(x2−4)2/40. Drag the slider to change inverse temperature β\betaβ. The red curve is the Boltzmann density; the dashed blue curve is the energy H(x)H(x)H(x). Higher β\betaβ concentrates mass on the minima.

This “known formula, no samples” setup appears across many fields, often with the same structure: a scoring function we can evaluate, and a normalizing constant we cannot compute.

  • Bayesian inference. The posterior p(θ∣D)∝p(D∣θ) p(θ)p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)p(θ∣D)∝p(D∣θ)p(θ) scores each parameter setting θ\thetaθ by how well it explains the data, but the marginal likelihood Z=∫p(D∣θ) p(θ) dθZ = \int p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\,d\thetaZ=∫p(D∣θ)p(θ)dθ is intractable.
  • Statistical physics. Equilibrium states of spin systems follow Boltzmann statistics. The partition function Z=∑xe−βH(x)Z = \sum_x e^{-\beta H(x)}Z=∑x​e−βH(x) sums over exponentially many configurations.
  • Combinatorial optimization. NP-hard problems can be recast as sampling from a Boltzmann distribution at low temperature, where the optimal solutions carry the most probability mass.

Notice the contrast with standard generative modeling (image generation, language models), where we have a dataset of samples but no formula for the density. Here the situation is reversed:

SettingSamples?Density?Goal
Data-based generative modelingYesNoLearn distribution from data
Data-free sampling (this post)NoYesSample from known unnormalized density

The question this post explores is whether diffusion models, originally built for the data-rich setting, can be adapted to sample from distributions specified only by a formula. The post has two parts. Section 2 covers differentiable targets in continuous space, where ∇log⁡π\nabla \log \pi∇logπ is available. Section 3 covers discrete or non-differentiable targets, where gradient-based Langevin dynamics no longer applies directly. The main practical lesson is deliberately modest: diffusion ideas are useful, but classical MCMC remains surprisingly competitive, and the strongest methods often mix neural and classical components.

Notation convention. π0\pi_0π0​ is the prior (noise) density, chosen so that we can sample from it and usually evaluate it. πT=π\pi_T = \piπT​=π is the target density, known only up to normalization. The forward process runs from t=0t=0t=0 to t=Tt=Tt=T, transporting samples from π0\pi_0π0​ toward πT\pi_TπT​. The backward (reference) process runs from t=Tt=Tt=T to t=0t=0t=0, noising the target back into the prior.

2. Differentiable targets

When the target lives in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd and we can compute ∇log⁡π(x)\nabla \log \pi(x)∇logπ(x), we have a powerful tool: the gradient tells us which direction to move to increase probability. All methods in this section build on this gradient, connecting an easy-to-sample prior π0\pi_0π0​ (usually a Gaussian) to the target πT=π\pi_T = \piπT​=π.

2.1 Classical methods

Metropolis-Hastings and detailed balance

Before introducing gradient-based samplers, we recall the most basic Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) idea. The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm (MH) generates a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is π\piπ. At each step, propose a move x′∼q(x′∣x)x' \sim q(x'\mid x)x′∼q(x′∣x) and accept it with probability

A(x′∣x)=min⁡ ⁣(1,  π(x′) q(x∣x′)π(x) q(x′∣x))A(x'\mid x) = \min\!\left(1,\;\frac{\pi(x')\,q(x\mid x')}{\pi(x)\,q(x'\mid x)}\right)A(x′∣x)=min(1,π(x)q(x′∣x)π(x′)q(x∣x′)​)

Notice that only the ratio π(x′)/π(x)\pi(x')/\pi(x)π(x′)/π(x) appears, so the intractable normalizing constant ZZZ cancels. The accept/reject rule is designed to enforce detailed balance:

π(x) T(x′∣x)=π(x′) T(x∣x′)\pi(x)\,T(x'\mid x) = \pi(x')\,T(x\mid x')π(x)T(x′∣x)=π(x′)T(x∣x′)

where T(x′∣x)=q(x′∣x) A(x′∣x)T(x'\mid x) = q(x'\mid x)\,A(x'\mid x)T(x′∣x)=q(x′∣x)A(x′∣x) is the overall transition kernel. Detailed balance says that the probability of being at xxx and jumping to x′x'x′ equals the probability of being at x′x'x′ and jumping to xxx. The chain is time-reversible. This immediately implies π\piπ is a stationary distribution: summing both sides over xxx gives π(x′)=∑xπ(x) T(x′∣x)\pi(x') = \sum_x \pi(x)\,T(x'\mid x)π(x′)=∑x​π(x)T(x′∣x).

Detailed balance. A transition kernel TTT satisfies detailed balance with respect to π\piπ if π(x)T(x′∣x)=π(x′)T(x∣x′)\pi(x)T(x'|x) = \pi(x')T(x|x')π(x)T(x′∣x)=π(x′)T(x∣x′) for all x,x′x,x'x,x′. This is stronger than stationarity (πT=π\pi T = \piπT=π). It additionally requires microscopic reversibility. Most MCMC methods are designed to satisfy detailed balance, though some non-reversible MCMC methods deliberately break it for faster mixing.

MH with a simple random-walk proposal q(x′∣x)=N(x′∣x,ϵ2I)q(x'\mid x) = \mathcal{N}(x'\mid x, \epsilon^2 I)q(x′∣x)=N(x′∣x,ϵ2I) works in any dimension but mixes slowly because the proposals ignore the geometry of π\piπ. The next algorithm fixes this by using the gradient.

Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA)

The core intuition behind ULA is simple. If you are standing on a landscape and want to find the peaks, walk uphill. The “landscape” here is log⁡π(x)\log \pi(x)logπ(x), and “uphill” means following ∇log⁡π(x)\nabla \log \pi(x)∇logπ(x). But if you only walk uphill, you will get stuck at the nearest peak and never explore other modes. So we add random noise to force exploration. This gives the Langevin stochastic differential equation (SDE):

dXt=∇log⁡π(Xt)⏟drift: walk uphill dt+2 dWt⏟noise: exploredX_t = \underbrace{\nabla \log \pi(X_t)}_{\text{drift: walk uphill}}\,dt + \underbrace{\sqrt{2}\,dW_t}_{\text{noise: explore}}dXt​=drift: walk uphill∇logπ(Xt​)​​dt+noise: explore2​dWt​​​

Let us unpack what this equation means. Xt∈RdX_t \in \mathbb{R}^dXt​∈Rd is the position of a particle at time ttt. The equation says that in an infinitesimal time interval dtdtdt, the particle moves by ∇log⁡π(Xt) dt\nabla \log \pi(X_t)\,dt∇logπ(Xt​)dt (a deterministic push toward higher density) plus 2 dWt\sqrt{2}\,dW_t2​dWt​ (a random Gaussian kick with variance 2 dt2\,dt2dt in each coordinate), where WtW_tWt​ is a standard ddd-dimensional Brownian motion.

Brownian motion. WtW_tWt​ is a continuous random process starting at W0=0W_0 = 0W0​=0 whose increments Wt+s−Wt∼N(0,sI)W_{t+s} - W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, sI)Wt+s​−Wt​∼N(0,sI) are independent Gaussians. It is the continuous-time limit of a random walk. In ddd dimensions, each coordinate is an independent 1D Brownian motion.

Under regularity conditions (smoothness, log-concavity or a Poincaré inequality), this SDE has π\piπ as its unique stationary distribution. The balance between drift and noise is exact. To verify this, substitute p=πp = \pip=π into the stationary Fokker-Planck equation 0=−∇⋅(p ∇log⁡π)+Δp0 = -\nabla \cdot (p\,\nabla \log \pi) + \Delta p0=−∇⋅(p∇logπ)+Δp:

−∇⋅(π∇log⁡π)+Δπ=−∇⋅(∇π)+Δπ=−Δπ+Δπ=0  ✓-\nabla \cdot (\pi \nabla \log \pi) + \Delta \pi = -\nabla \cdot (\nabla \pi) + \Delta \pi = -\Delta \pi + \Delta \pi = 0 \;\checkmark−∇⋅(π∇logπ)+Δπ=−∇⋅(∇π)+Δπ=−Δπ+Δπ=0✓

Fokker-Planck equation. If particles are distributed with density p(x,t)p(x,t)p(x,t) and each follows the SDE dXt=μ dt+σ dWtdX_t = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW_tdXt​=μdt+σdWt​, then ppp evolves as ∂tp=−∇⋅(pμ)+σ22Δp\partial_t p = -\nabla \cdot (p\mu) + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta p∂t​p=−∇⋅(pμ)+2σ2​Δp. The first term is advection (drift carries density); the second is diffusion (noise spreads density). At steady state (∂tp=0\partial_t p = 0∂t​p=0), the density no longer changes. For the Langevin SDE above, σ=2\sigma = \sqrt{2}σ=2​, so the diffusion coefficient is σ2/2=1\sigma^2/2 = 1σ2/2=1 and the steady-state equation reduces to 0=−∇⋅(p ∇log⁡π)+Δp0 = -\nabla \cdot (p\,\nabla \log \pi) + \Delta p0=−∇⋅(p∇logπ)+Δp.

The first equality uses the identity π∇log⁡π=π∇π/π=∇π\pi \nabla \log \pi = \pi \nabla\pi / \pi = \nabla\piπ∇logπ=π∇π/π=∇π.

Euler-Maruyama. Just as Euler’s method discretizes ODEs (xn+1=xn+f(xn)Δtx_{n+1} = x_n + f(x_n)\Delta txn+1​=xn​+f(xn​)Δt), Euler-Maruyama discretizes SDEs by adding a noise term: Xn+1=Xn+μ(Xn)Δt+σΔt ξnX_{n+1} = X_n + \mu(X_n)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\xi_nXn+1​=Xn​+μ(Xn​)Δt+σΔt​ξn​ where ξn∼N(0,I)\xi_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)ξn​∼N(0,I). The Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ scaling (not Δt\Delta tΔt) comes from the fact that Brownian increments have standard deviation Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​.

In practice we discretize with step size hhh, giving the ULA update:

Xt+1=Xt+h ∇log⁡π(Xt)+2h  zt,zt∼N(0,I)X_{t+1} = X_t + h\,\nabla \log \pi(X_t) + \sqrt{2h}\;z_t, \qquad z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)Xt+1​=Xt​+h∇logπ(Xt​)+2h​zt​,zt​∼N(0,I)

This introduces discretization bias: the chain’s stationary distribution is no longer exactly π\piπ. For smooth targets and stable step sizes, the bias in expectations is typically first order in hhh, often written O(h)O(h)O(h). This is an asymptotic statement, not a guarantee that any large step is merely “a bit less accurate.” The bias arises because the Euler-Maruyama step evaluates the score ∇log⁡π\nabla \log \pi∇logπ at the current point and treats it as constant over the interval, while the true continuous dynamics follows a varying score along a curved path.

Changing hhh also changes how far the chain can move in one step. The noise term 2h zt\sqrt{2h}\,z_t2h​zt​ has standard deviation proportional to h\sqrt{h}h​, so a larger step can sometimes jump across a low-density barrier that a smaller step would rarely cross. But this is not free exploration. It is partly an artifact of the discretization, and if hhh is too large the chain can become badly biased or unstable. Figure 2 is meant to show this practical tension: small hhh follows the local geometry more faithfully but may stay in one mode for a long time; large hhh moves farther but no longer approximates the target well.

The Metropolis-Adjusted Langevin Algorithm (MALA) fixes the discretization bias by wrapping each ULA proposal in a Metropolis-Hastings accept/reject step. This restores π\piπ as the exact stationary distribution, but rejected moves become more common as hhh grows. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) takes a different approach. It introduces auxiliary momentum variables vvv and simulates the Hamiltonian system x˙=v\dot{x} = vx˙=v, v˙=−∇H(x)\dot{v} = -\nabla H(x)v˙=−∇H(x) using leapfrog integration, producing distant proposals that reduce random-walk behavior.

Figure 2. ULA on a 4-mode Gaussian mixture. Four independent runs (500 steps each) start from different corners. Adjust step size hhh, then click Run ULA. Small hhh follows local geometry more faithfully but often stays in one mode. Large hhh moves farther, sometimes crossing modes, but can introduce substantial bias.

All these methods rely on hand-crafted transition kernels with fixed step sizes and noise schedules.

Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS)

ULA’s problem is clear from Figure 2: the particle gets trapped near whichever mode it starts closest to. The noise helps locally, but crossing the low-density valley between modes is exponentially unlikely.

AIS [1]Neal, R. M. (2001). Annealed Importance Sampling. Statistics and Computing, 11, 125--139. attacks this differently. Instead of sampling from the hard target directly, build a bridge of easy-to-hard distributions. Start with the Gaussian prior (easy), and gradually morph it into the target (hard):

πt(x)=π0(x)1−βt  πT(x)βt,0=β0<β1<⋯<βT=1\pi_t(x) = \pi_0(x)^{1-\beta_t}\;\pi_T(x)^{\beta_t}, \qquad 0 = \beta_0 < \beta_1 < \cdots < \beta_T = 1πt​(x)=π0​(x)1−βt​πT​(x)βt​,0=β0​<β1​<⋯<βT​=1

When βt≈0\beta_t \approx 0βt​≈0, the distribution is nearly Gaussian and the modes have not formed yet, so particles can move freely. As βt\beta_tβt​ increases, the modes sharpen. If the schedule is slow enough, particles that started in different regions of the Gaussian will end up in different modes of the target.

Figure 3. Geometric interpolation between a Gaussian prior and a bimodal target. Drag the slider through the annealing steps. The equation at top shows the current interpolation. At t=0t=0t=0 the distribution is the Gaussian prior; at t=Tt=Tt=T it is the target.

AIS alternates two operations: reweight for the change from one intermediate density to the next, then apply an MCMC transition that leaves the new intermediate density invariant. One common indexing is:

w=∏t=1Tπt(xt−1)πt−1(xt−1),xt∼Ft(⋅∣xt−1),Ft leaves πt invariant.w = \prod_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\pi_t(x_{t-1})}{\pi_{t-1}(x_{t-1})}, \qquad x_t \sim F_t(\cdot \mid x_{t-1}), \quad F_t \text{ leaves } \pi_t \text{ invariant}.w=t=1∏T​πt−1​(xt−1​)πt​(xt−1​)​,xt​∼Ft​(⋅∣xt−1​),Ft​ leaves πt​ invariant.

The transition kernel does not by itself transport an exact πt−1\pi_{t-1}πt−1​ sample into an exact πt\pi_tπt​ sample; it only helps the particle equilibrate after the temperature change. The importance weight corrects the remaining mismatch. With unnormalized intermediate densities, www is an unbiased estimator of ZT/Z0Z_T/Z_0ZT​/Z0​. When the prior is normalized (Z0=1Z_0=1Z0​=1), E[w]=ZT\mathbb{E}[w]=Z_TE[w]=ZT​. The variational interpretation is that E[log⁡w]\mathbb{E}[\log w]E[logw] is an evidence lower bound (ELBO) on log⁡ZT\log Z_TlogZT​, since Jensen’s inequality gives log⁡E[w]≥E[log⁡w]\log \mathbb{E}[w] \geq \mathbb{E}[\log w]logE[w]≥E[logw].

From classical to modern samplers

ULA gives us gradient-guided dynamics but gets trapped. AIS gives us bridging distributions and importance weighting but relies on hand-crafted kernels. The idea behind modern diffusion-based samplers is to combine the best of both: continuous-time Langevin-like SDEs flowing along an annealing path, with the transition kernel either learned by a neural network or estimated on the fly using Monte Carlo techniques.

In fact, the escorted transport SDE (§2.2) with the learned drift set to zero (fθ=0f_\theta = 0fθ​=0) can be viewed as a continuous-time analogue of AIS with Langevin kernels along the annealing path. The learned fθf_\thetafθ​ tries to add a transport correction that hand-crafted AIS kernels do not provide. Some recent methods replace the neural network entirely with SMC-based score estimation, showing that the diffusion path framework can be useful even without learned components (we will see one such method, DPSMC, in §2.5).

2.2 Sampling processes

Following the unified framework summarized by He et al. [2]He, J., Du, Y., Vargas, F., Zhang, D., Padhy, S., OuYang, R., Gomes, C., Hernandez-Lobato, J. M. (2025). No Trick, No Treat: Pursuits and Challenges Towards Simulation-free Training of Neural Samplers. arXiv:2502.06685, the continuous diffusion samplers discussed here can be written in a common SDE form:

dXt=[μt(Xt)+σt2 bt(Xt)] dt+σt2 dWt,X0∼ppriordX_t = \bigl[\mu_t(X_t) + \sigma_t^2\,b_t(X_t)\bigr]\,dt + \sigma_t\sqrt{2}\,dW_t, \qquad X_0 \sim p_{\text{prior}}dXt​=[μt​(Xt​)+σt2​bt​(Xt​)]dt+σt​2​dWt​,X0​∼pprior​

Here μt\mu_tμt​ is a drift, btb_tbt​ is a control or score term, and σt\sigma_tσt​ is the diffusion coefficient. Different methods arise from different choices of what to fix and what to learn among {μt,σt,bt,pprior}\{\mu_t, \sigma_t, b_t, p_{\text{prior}}\}{μt​,σt​,bt​,pprior​}.

Figure 4. VP-SDE (Euler-Maruyama discretization) on a bimodal 1D target. The horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is space, and the background shading shows the analytical marginal density. Red trajectories show forward (noising) paths from the target toward the prior. Blue trajectories show a second independent set of noising paths, displayed in reverse time to illustrate what the backward (denoising) direction looks like. Both sets use the same OU noising SDE; the true reverse SDE would require a learned score and is not simulated here.

Two paradigms are useful to keep separate: time-reversal and escorted transport. Time-reversal methods choose a noising process and learn how to reverse it. Escorted transport methods choose an annealing path and learn a correction that keeps particles close to that path. Section 2.3 then explains the losses used to train the learned parts.

Time-reversal samplers

The idea is to define a backward reference process that destroys a target sample into noise, then learn to reverse it. The key mathematical tool is Anderson’s theorem, which gives the exact form of the reversed SDE.

Anderson’s theorem [3]Anderson, B. D. O. (1982). Reverse-time diffusion equation models. Stochastic Processes and their Applications, 12, 313--326.. For any Itô diffusion dXt=f(Xt,t) dt+g(t) dWtdX_t = f(X_t, t)\,dt + g(t)\,dW_tdXt​=f(Xt​,t)dt+g(t)dWt​ with marginal density ptp_tpt​, the time-reversed process satisfies dXˉt=[−f(Xˉt,T−t)+g(T−t) g(T−t)⊤∇log⁡pT−t(Xˉt)] dt+g(T−t) dWˉtd\bar{X}_t = [-f(\bar{X}_t, T{-}t) + g(T{-}t)\,g(T{-}t)^\top \nabla \log p_{T-t}(\bar{X}_t)]\,dt + g(T{-}t)\,d\bar{W}_tdXˉt​=[−f(Xˉt​,T−t)+g(T−t)g(T−t)⊤∇logpT−t​(Xˉt​)]dt+g(T−t)dWˉt​. The reversed drift has two parts: −f-f−f undoes the original drift, and gg⊤∇log⁡pT−tgg^\top \nabla \log p_{T-t}gg⊤∇logpT−t​ is a score correction accounting for the irreversibility of Brownian motion.

Applying Anderson’s theorem to a chosen reference process gives us the forward (generative) SDE. The score ∇log⁡pT−t\nabla \log p_{T-t}∇logpT−t​ appearing in the reversed drift is intractable because we have no samples from the backward marginals, so it is the quantity the neural network must learn. In data-based generative modeling [4]Song, Y., Sohl-Dickstein, J., Kingma, D. P., Kumar, A., Ermon, S., Poole, B. (2021). Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations. ICLR. arXiv:2011.13456, this score is learned from noisy data pairs via denoising score matching [5, 6]Vincent, P. (2011). A Connection Between Score Matching and Denoising Autoencoders. Neural Computation, 23, 1661--1674.

Song, Y., Ermon, S. (2019). Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 32. arXiv:1907.05600. In data-free sampling, the same formula applies, but the score must be learned indirectly through path-space divergences or optimal control objectives (§2.3).

Three reference processes are used in practice:

The variance-preserving SDE (VP-SDE) is used by Denoising Diffusion Sampler (DDS) [7]Vargas, F., Grathwohl, W., Doucet, A. (2023). Denoising Diffusion Samplers. dYt=−βtYt dt+v2βt dWt,Y0∼πTdY_t = -\beta_t Y_t\,dt + v\sqrt{2\beta_t}\,dW_t, \qquad Y_0 \sim \pi_TdYt​=−βt​Yt​dt+v2βt​​dWt​,Y0​∼πT​

Here v>0v > 0v>0 is a scalar controlling the terminal variance. This is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Together they drive any initial distribution toward N(0,v2I)\mathcal{N}(0, v^2 I)N(0,v2I).

Applying Anderson’s theorem with f(x,t)=−βtxf(x,t) = -\beta_t xf(x,t)=−βt​x and g(t)=v2βtg(t) = v\sqrt{2\beta_t}g(t)=v2βt​​, so gg⊤=2v2βtIgg^\top = 2v^2\beta_t Igg⊤=2v2βt​I, the time-reversed forward SDE is:

dXt=βT−tXt dt+2v2βT−t bθ(Xt,t) dt+v2βT−t dWt,X0∼N(0,v2I)dX_t = \beta_{T-t} X_t\,dt + 2v^2\beta_{T-t}\,b_\theta(X_t, t)\,dt + v\sqrt{2\beta_{T-t}}\,dW_t, \qquad X_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, v^2 I)dXt​=βT−t​Xt​dt+2v2βT−t​bθ​(Xt​,t)dt+v2βT−t​​dWt​,X0​∼N(0,v2I)

where bθ(x,t)≈∇log⁡pT−t(x)b_\theta(x,t) \approx \nabla \log p_{T-t}(x)bθ​(x,t)≈∇logpT−t​(x) is the neural network approximation to the intractable score.

The variance-exploding SDE (VE-SDE) is used by Iterated Denoising Energy Matching (iDEM) [9]Akhound-Sadegh, T., Rector-Brooks, J., Bose, J., Mittal, S., Lemos, P., Liu, C., Sendera, M., Ravanbakhsh, S., Gidel, G., Bengio, Y., Malkin, N., Tong, A. (2024). Iterated Denoising Energy Matching for Sampling from Boltzmann Densities. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 760--786. arXiv:2402.06121:

dYt=g(t) dWt,Y0∼πTdY_t = g(t)\,dW_t, \qquad Y_0 \sim \pi_TdYt​=g(t)dWt​,Y0​∼πT​

Pure diffusion with no drift and a time-dependent diffusion coefficient g(t)g(t)g(t). The marginal variance σt2=∫0tg(s)2 ds\sigma_t^2 = \int_0^t g(s)^2\,dsσt2​=∫0t​g(s)2ds grows without bound, hence “variance exploding.” A common choice is g(t)=2tg(t) = \sqrt{2t}g(t)=2t​, giving σt2=t2\sigma_t^2 = t^2σt2​=t2. iDEM estimates the score via a Target Score Identity using self-normalized importance sampling, avoiding path-space divergences entirely.

Pinned Brownian motion (PBM) is used by Path Integral Sampler (PIS) [10]Zhang, Q., Chen, Y. (2022). Path Integral Sampler: A Stochastic Control Approach for Sampling. ICLR. arXiv:2111.15141:

dYt=−YtT−t dt+dWt,Y0∼πTdY_t = -\frac{Y_t}{T-t}\,dt + dW_t, \qquad Y_0 \sim \pi_TdYt​=−T−tYt​​dt+dWt​,Y0​∼πT​

This is a Brownian bridge pinned to 0 at time TTT, so the terminal distribution is δ0\delta_0δ0​. Because the endpoint is fixed, PBM is not an ergodic reference process in the usual MCMC sense and gives less opportunity for global mixing than an OU reference. PIS corrects for suboptimal control via Girsanov-based path integral importance weights.

Reference processSDETerminal distributionMethods
VP-SDEdY=−βtY dt+v2βt dWdY = -\beta_t Y\,dt + v\sqrt{2\beta_t}\,dWdY=−βt​Ydt+v2βt​​dWN(0,v2I)\mathcal{N}(0, v^2 I)N(0,v2I)DDS, DIS
VE-SDEdY=g(t) dWdY = g(t)\,dWdY=g(t)dW≈N(0,σT2I)\approx\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_T^2 I)≈N(0,σT2​I)iDEM
PBMdY=−Y/(T−t) dt+dWdY = -Y/(T{-}t)\,dt + dWdY=−Y/(T−t)dt+dWδ0\delta_0δ0​PIS

Each choice has tradeoffs. The VP-SDE has an ergodic OU reference and a fixed Gaussian prior, but mode allocation is still difficult because the reverse sampler must learn where each noisy particle should denoise. The VE-SDE is the simplest but often requires many diffusion steps because it has no mean-reverting drift. PBM allows a delta-function prior, which can be useful when the target is concentrated, but the pinned endpoint limits mixing.

Escorted transport

Instead of reversing a noising process, escorted transport methods prescribe a sequence of intermediate marginal densities, typically the AIS geometric interpolation πt=π01−βtπTβt\pi_t = \pi_0^{1-\beta_t}\pi_T^{\beta_t}πt​=π01−βt​​πTβt​​, and learn a drift that makes the SDE’s actual marginals track them. The score of πt\pi_tπt​ is available analytically. Since log⁡πt=(1−βt)log⁡π0+βtlog⁡πT\log \pi_t = (1-\beta_t)\log \pi_0 + \beta_t \log \pi_Tlogπt​=(1−βt​)logπ0​+βt​logπT​, we get:

∇log⁡πt(x)=(1−βt) ∇log⁡π0(x)+βt ∇log⁡πT(x)\nabla \log \pi_t(x) = (1-\beta_t)\,\nabla \log \pi_0(x) + \beta_t\,\nabla \log \pi_T(x)∇logπt​(x)=(1−βt​)∇logπ0​(x)+βt​∇logπT​(x)

The general escorted transport SDE is:

dXt=[fθ(Xt,t)+σt2 ∇log⁡πt(Xt)] dt+σt2 dWt,X0∼π0dX_t = \bigl[f_\theta(X_t, t) + \sigma_t^2\,\nabla \log \pi_t(X_t)\bigr]\,dt + \sigma_t\sqrt{2}\,dW_t, \qquad X_0 \sim \pi_0dXt​=[fθ​(Xt​,t)+σt2​∇logπt​(Xt​)]dt+σt​2​dWt​,X0​∼π0​

where fθf_\thetafθ​ is the learned control drift. If the marginals of XtX_tXt​ match πt\pi_tπt​ exactly, Nelson’s identity gives the backward drift directly, with no reverse simulation needed.

Nelson’s identity [11]Nelson, E. (1967). Dynamical Theories of Brownian Motion. Princeton University Press.. For an SDE written in this post’s convention, dXt=μ⃗→dt+2σ(t)dWtdX_t=\vec\mu_\rightarrow dt+\sqrt{2}\sigma(t)dW_tdXt​=μ​→​dt+2​σ(t)dWt​, the backward drift is μ⃗←(x,t)=μ⃗→(x,t)−2σ(t)2∇log⁡p(x,t)\vec\mu_\leftarrow(x,t)=\vec\mu_\rightarrow(x,t)-2\sigma(t)^2\nabla\log p(x,t)μ​←​(x,t)=μ​→​(x,t)−2σ(t)2∇logp(x,t), where p(x,t)p(x,t)p(x,t) is the marginal density. If instead the SDE is written as dXt=μdt+σdWtdX_t=\mu dt+\sigma dW_tdXt​=μdt+σdWt​, the factor is σ2\sigma^2σ2. Unlike Anderson’s theorem (which gives the full reversed SDE), this is a pointwise algebraic relation. It is especially useful when p(⋅,t)p(\cdot,t)p(⋅,t) is known analytically.

When p(⋅,t)=πtp(\cdot, t) = \pi_tp(⋅,t)=πt​, Nelson’s identity gives μ⃗←=fθ−σt2∇log⁡πt\vec\mu_\leftarrow = f_\theta - \sigma_t^2 \nabla \log \pi_tμ​←​=fθ​−σt2​∇logπt​, so the backward SDE is fully determined by the forward one.

Setting fθ=0f_\theta = 0fθ​=0 gives overdamped Langevin dynamics targeting the current πt\pi_tπt​, the continuous-time counterpart of an AIS baseline with ULA-style kernels. The learned fθf_\thetafθ​ is a transport correction on top of this baseline. Controlled Monte Carlo Diffusion (CMCD) [12]Vargas, F., Padhy, S., Blessing, D., Nusken, N. (2024). Transport Meets Variational Inference: Controlled Monte Carlo Diffusions. ICLR. arXiv:2307.01050 parameterizes fθ=∇φθf_\theta = \nabla\varphi_\thetafθ​=∇φθ​ as the gradient of a potential. Non-Equilibrium Transport Sampler (NETS) [13]Albergo, M. S., Vanden-Eijnden, E. (2024). NETS: A Non-Equilibrium Transport Sampler. arXiv:2410.02711 uses mode-based interpolation. The Schrödinger bridge (SB) perspective

The sampling processes above, both time-reversal and escorted transport, can be unified under the framework of the Schrödinger bridge (SB) problem [15, 16]Leonard, C. (2014). A Survey of the Schrodinger Problem and Some of Its Connections with Optimal Transport. Discrete and Continuous Dynamical Systems, 34, 1533--1574.

De Bortoli, V., Thornton, J., Heng, J., Doucet, A. (2021). Diffusion Schrodinger Bridge with Applications to Score-Based Generative Modeling. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 34, 17695--17709. arXiv:2106.01357. A Schrödinger bridge is the stochastic process that transports one distribution (the prior) to another (the target) while staying as close as possible to a reference process, measured by the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence on path space:

p∗=arg⁡min⁡p: p0=π0, pT=πTDKL(p∥pref)p^* = \arg\min_{p:\, p_0 = \pi_0,\, p_T = \pi_T} D_{\text{KL}}(p \| p^{\text{ref}})p∗=argp:p0​=π0​,pT​=πT​min​DKL​(p∥pref)

where prefp^{\text{ref}}pref is the path measure of the reference dynamics (e.g. Brownian motion). The optimal process p∗p^*p∗ has the same diffusion coefficient as the reference but a modified drift, which can be characterized via a pair of Schrödinger potentials (φt,φ^t)(\varphi_t, \hat\varphi_t)(φt​,φ^​t​) satisfying coupled forward-backward equations.

Connection to stochastic optimal control (SOC). The SB problem is equivalent to a stochastic optimal control problem with running cost 12σ2∥u∥2\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|u\|^22σ21​∥u∥2 and terminal cost encoding the target constraint. The optimal control u∗=−σ2∇Vu^* = -\sigma^2 \nabla Vu∗=−σ2∇V satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. This connection, established by Dai Pra [17]Dai Pra, P. (1991). A stochastic control approach to reciprocal diffusion processes. Applied Mathematics and Optimization, 23, 313--329. and developed by Chen et al., is what allows diffusion samplers to borrow machinery from optimal control theory.

Richter & Berner [18]Richter, L., Berner, J. (2024). Improved Sampling via Learned Diffusions. ICLR. arXiv:2307.01198 proved that DDS, DIS, PIS, and CMCD are all special cases of this generalized SB problem. Different methods correspond to different choices of reference dynamics and parameterizations. The deterministic limit (σt=0\sigma_t = 0σt​=0, i.e. LFIS) parallels the probability flow ODE from Song et al. [4]Song, Y., Sohl-Dickstein, J., Kingma, D. P., Kumar, A., Ermon, S., Poole, B. (2021). Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations. ICLR. arXiv:2011.13456 and connects to flow matching [19]Lipman, Y., Chen, R. T. Q., Ben-Hamu, H., Nickel, M., Le, M. (2023). Flow Matching for Generative Modeling. ICLR. arXiv:2210.02747. This perspective will reappear in §3.5 when we extend SB theory to discrete state spaces.

The marginal density p(x,t)p(x,t)p(x,t) evolves according to the Fokker-Planck equation:

∂tp=−∇⋅(p μ⃗→)+σ2Δp,p(⋅,0)=pprior\partial_t p = -\nabla \cdot (p\,\vec\mu_\rightarrow) + \sigma^2\Delta p, \qquad p(\cdot, 0) = p_{\text{prior}}∂t​p=−∇⋅(pμ​→​)+σ2Δp,p(⋅,0)=pprior​

This PDE expresses conservation of probability mass under stochastic transport. Informally, it plays the same bookkeeping role as the flow conservation equation that will appear in GFlowNets (§3.3): probability cannot disappear; it can only move or diffuse.

Comparing the two paradigms

Time-reversalEscorted transport
What is learnedScore bθ≈∇log⁡pT−tb_\theta \approx \nabla \log p_{T-t}bθ​≈∇logpT−t​Control drift fθf_\thetafθ​
What is fixedDrift from reference SDEScore ∇log⁡πt\nabla \log \pi_t∇logπt​ (analytic)

Langevin preconditioningMust be added explicitlyBuilt in via σt2∇log⁡πt\sigma_t^2 \nabla \log \pi_tσt2​∇logπt​

The practical distinction is simple: time-reversal methods learn an unknown noisy-target score, while escorted methods choose the intermediate targets and learn a correction on top of a Langevin-like baseline.

2.3 Training objectives

The sampling process (§2.2) defines how particles move; the training objective defines what is optimized to make those particles follow the right distribution. For methods with learned components (neural networks), the objective guides gradient updates. Many objectives in this field can be written in terms of a single object: the log-ratio between the forward and backward path measures, called the Radon-Nikodym derivative (RND).

The log-RND

Suppose we run the learned forward SDE from prior to target, producing a trajectory X^=(X^0,X^1,…,X^N)\hat{X} = (\hat{X}_0, \hat{X}_1, \ldots, \hat{X}_N)X^=(X^0​,X^1​,…,X^N​). If the sampler were perfect, the forward and backward path measures would agree after accounting for the target’s unknown normalizing constant. The log-RND measures the remaining discrepancy:

R(X^)=log⁡dP^dQ^(X^)R(\hat{X}) = \log \frac{d\hat{\mathbb{P}}}{d\hat{\mathbb{Q}}}(\hat{X})R(X^)=logdQ^​dP^​(X^)

For normalized endpoint densities, exact path matching would make R=0R = 0R=0 everywhere. With an unnormalized target, the best we can generally hope for is that RRR is constant across paths; that constant contains the missing normalizing constant. This is why many objectives below try to reduce the variance of RRR, not necessarily its raw value.

Computing RRR in continuous time. For two SDEs sharing the same diffusion coefficient σ(t)\sigma(t)σ(t) but with different drifts μ⃗(1),μ⃗(2)\vec\mu^{(1)}, \vec\mu^{(2)}μ​(1),μ​(2), Girsanov’s theorem gives:

log⁡dP(1)dP(2)(X)=∫01∥μ⃗(2)∥2−∥μ⃗(1)∥22σ(t)2 dt+∫01μ⃗(1)−μ⃗(2)σ(t)2⋅dXt\log \frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(1)}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(2)}}(X) = \int_0^1 \frac{\|\vec\mu^{(2)}\|^2 - \|\vec\mu^{(1)}\|^2}{2\sigma(t)^2}\,dt + \int_0^1 \frac{\vec\mu^{(1)} - \vec\mu^{(2)}}{\sigma(t)^2} \cdot dX_tlogdP(2)dP(1)​(X)=∫01​2σ(t)2∥μ​(2)∥2−∥μ​(1)∥2​dt+∫01​σ(t)2μ​(1)−μ​(2)​⋅dXt​

The first integral is a standard Riemann integral. The second is an Itô integral. It depends on the actual stochastic path XXX takes, not just its endpoints. Intuitively, changing the drift of an SDE is equivalent to reweighting the path measure by an exponential martingale.

Itô integral. ∫0Tf(Xt) dWt\int_0^T f(X_t)\,dW_t∫0T​f(Xt​)dWt​ is the continuous-time limit of ∑nf(Xtn)(Wtn+1−Wtn)\sum_n f(X_{t_n})(W_{t_{n+1}} - W_{t_n})∑n​f(Xtn​​)(Wtn+1​​−Wtn​​). Its expected value is zero (it is a martingale), but its variance is ∫0T∥f(Xt)∥2 dt\int_0^T \|f(X_t)\|^2\,dt∫0T​∥f(Xt​)∥2dt.

Global objectives

Every global objective takes the log-RND R(X^)R(\hat{X})R(X^) and penalizes it for not being constant. The three main choices differ in how they do this:

Reverse KL. LKL=EP^[R]\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}}[R]LKL​=EP^​[R]. Minimizes the expected log-ratio. This is mode-seeking: the model can achieve low loss by covering just one mode well and ignoring the rest, because missing a mode does not increase E[R]\mathbb{E}[R]E[R]. Gradients require backpropagating through the SDE solver (reparameterization trick), which can be numerically unstable for long trajectories. Used by PIS [10]Zhang, Q., Chen, Y. (2022). Path Integral Sampler: A Stochastic Control Approach for Sampling. ICLR. arXiv:2111.15141 and DIS [8]Berner, J., Richter, L., Ullrich, K. (2024). An Optimal Control Perspective on Diffusion-Based Generative Modeling. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2211.01364.

Log-variance (LV). LLV=VarW^[R]\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}} = \text{Var}_{\hat{\mathbb{W}}}[R]LLV​=VarW^​[R]. Penalizes the variance of the log-ratio. When W^=P^\hat{\mathbb{W}} = \hat{\mathbb{P}}W^=P^ (on-policy), the gradient of LV is proportional to the REINFORCE gradient of the reverse KL [22, 20]Richter, L., Boustati, A., Nusken, N., Ruiz, F., Akyildiz, O. D. (2020). VarGrad: A Low-Variance Gradient Estimator for Variational Inference. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33.

Berner, J., Richter, L., Sendera, M., Rector-Brooks, J., Malkin, N. (2026). From Discrete-Time Policies to Continuous-Time Diffusion Samplers: Asymptotic Equivalences and Faster Training. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2501.06148. But LV does not require backprop through the SDE solver; it uses a REINFORCE-like estimator with a built-in control variate. It also supports off-policy training (sampling from a replay buffer or mixture distribution). Empirically, LV tends to be more mode-covering than the reverse KL. Originally introduced as VarGrad [22]Richter, L., Boustati, A., Nusken, N., Ruiz, F., Akyildiz, O. D. (2020). VarGrad: A Low-Variance Gradient Estimator for Variational Inference. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33. for variational inference.

Trajectory balance (TB) / second moment. In the SDE literature [20]Berner, J., Richter, L., Sendera, M., Rector-Brooks, J., Malkin, N. (2026). From Discrete-Time Policies to Continuous-Time Diffusion Samplers: Asymptotic Equivalences and Faster Training. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2501.06148, TB often refers to a second-moment objective such as DTB=EW^[R2]D_{\text{TB}} = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{W}}}[R^2]DTB​=EW^​[R2], while LV is the centered version Var[R]\text{Var}[R]Var[R]. They are related by E[R2]=Var[R]+(E[R])2\mathbb{E}[R^2] = \text{Var}[R] + (\mathbb{E}[R])^2E[R2]=Var[R]+(E[R])2, so they coincide only when the centering constant is chosen appropriately. In the GFlowNet literature [23]Malkin, N., Jain, M., Bengio, E., Sun, C., Bengio, Y. (2022). Trajectory Balance: Improved Credit Assignment in GFlowNets. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 35, 5955--5967. arXiv:2201.13259, TB is written as LTB=EW^[(R−c)2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{TB}} = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{W}}}[(R - c)^2]LTB​=EW^​[(R−c)2] where ccc is a learned scalar estimating log⁡Z\log ZlogZ; using a batch-level centering estimate recovers an LV-style objective. TB originated in GFlowNets [23]Malkin, N., Jain, M., Bengio, E., Sun, C., Bengio, Y. (2022). Trajectory Balance: Improved Credit Assignment in GFlowNets. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 35, 5955--5967. arXiv:2201.13259 for discrete combinatorial sampling; Berner et al. [20]Berner, J., Richter, L., Sendera, M., Rector-Brooks, J., Malkin, N. (2026). From Discrete-Time Policies to Continuous-Time Diffusion Samplers: Asymptotic Equivalences and Faster Training. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2501.06148 proved asymptotic links between discrete-time TB-style losses and continuous-time path-space divergences as the time discretization becomes finer.

Forward KL vs reverse KL

The reverse KL DKL(P∥Q)D_{\text{KL}}(\mathbb{P}\|\mathbb{Q})DKL​(P∥Q) is the natural default because we can sample from P\mathbb{P}P (run the learned SDE) but not from Q\mathbb{Q}Q (which starts at the unknown target). It is mode-seeking: the model can achieve low loss by covering a few modes well and ignoring the rest.

The forward KL DKL(Q∥P)D_{\text{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P})DKL​(Q∥P) would be mode-covering but requires target samples we do not have. Recent work shows that some common explanations of LV’s advantage over rKL are incomplete. Sanokowski et al. [24]Sanokowski, S., Gruber, L., Bartmann, C., Hochreiter, S., Lehner, S. (2025). Rethinking Losses for Diffusion Bridge Samplers. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. arXiv:2506.10982 argue that, for diffusion bridge samplers, LV lacks the same data-processing motivation as KL objectives, and that part of rKL’s poor reputation comes from unstable gradients when rKL is optimized by backpropagating through long SDE trajectories. They propose rKL with the log-derivative trick (rKL-LD), which avoids backpropagating through the solver and performs strongly in their diffusion-bridge experiments.

In practice, empirical results are mixed: neither direction consistently dominates. The reverse KL can mode-collapse on multimodal targets, while forward-KL approximations introduce their own biases. The LV/TB losses, which are not pure KL divergences, often perform competitively in practice. The best choice depends on the specific problem and implementation details.

There is also a theoretical caveat: the path-space KL upper-bounds the marginal KL at time TTT by the data processing inequality [20]Berner, J., Richter, L., Sendera, M., Rector-Brooks, J., Malkin, N. (2026). From Discrete-Time Policies to Continuous-Time Diffusion Samplers: Asymptotic Equivalences and Faster Training. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2501.06148. Non-KL divergences like LV and TB do not satisfy this, so minimizing path-space LV does not guarantee the endpoint marginal is close to the target.

Local objectives

The log-RND telescopes. By introducing intermediate densities p^n\hat{p}_np^​n​ (learned or prescribed, e.g. p^n=π01−βnπTβn\hat{p}_n = \pi_0^{1-\beta_n}\pi_T^{\beta_n}p^​n​=π01−βn​​πTβn​​), we decompose RRR into per-step contributions:

R(X^)=∑n=0N−1log⁡p^n(X^n) π→,n(X^n+1∣X^n)p^n+1(X^n+1) π←,n+1(X^n∣X^n+1)⏟ΔnR(\hat{X}) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \underbrace{\log \frac{\hat{p}_n(\hat{X}_n)\,\pi_{\rightarrow,n}(\hat{X}_{n+1}\mid \hat{X}_n)}{\hat{p}_{n+1}(\hat{X}_{n+1})\,\pi_{\leftarrow,n+1}(\hat{X}_n\mid \hat{X}_{n+1})}}_{\Delta_n}R(X^)=n=0∑N−1​Δn​logp^​n+1​(X^n+1​)π←,n+1​(X^n​∣X^n+1​)p^​n​(X^n​)π→,n​(X^n+1​∣X^n​)​​​

with p^0=pprior\hat{p}_0 = p_{\text{prior}}p^​0​=pprior​ and p^N=ptarget\hat{p}_N = p_{\text{target}}p^​N​=ptarget​. This gives a family of losses at different granularities:

  • Detailed balance (DB): penalize each step independently, LDB=∑nE[Δn2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{DB}} = \sum_n \mathbb{E}[\Delta_n^2]LDB​=∑n​E[Δn2​]. Finest-grained; provides learning signal at every time step.
  • Sub-trajectory balance (STB): penalize sums over sub-trajectories, LSTB=∑i<jE[(∑n=ij−1Δn)2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{STB}} = \sum_{i < j} \mathbb{E}[(\sum_{n=i}^{j-1} \Delta_n)^2]LSTB​=∑i<j​E[(∑n=ij−1​Δn​)2].
  • Trajectory balance (TB): the special case i=0,j=Ni=0, j=Ni=0,j=N, penalizing the full sum.

DB is the most local, TB the most global, STB interpolates. Diffusion Generative Flow Sampler (DGFS) [25]Zhang, D., Chen, R. T. Q., Liu, C., Courville, A., Bengio, Y. (2024). Simulation-free objectives

The objectives above all require simulating the SDE to generate trajectories. Two alternatives avoid this:

PINN loss. Directly penalizes violations of the Fokker-Planck PDE at sampled points (x,t)(x, t)(x,t), without simulating the SDE. It is simulation-free and off-policy, but requires computing ∇⋅fθ\nabla \cdot f_\theta∇⋅fθ​ (the divergence of the network), which is expensive in high dimensions.

Score matching via Denoising Energy Matching (iDEM). The key idea is to express the intractable score ∇log⁡pt(xt)\nabla \log p_t(x_t)∇logpt​(xt​) as a ratio of expectations over Gaussian noise samples, then estimate it by Monte Carlo. Concretely, for a VE-SDE with noise level σt\sigma_tσt​, iDEM [9]Akhound-Sadegh, T., Rector-Brooks, J., Bose, J., Mittal, S., Lemos, P., Liu, C., Sendera, M., Ravanbakhsh, S., Gidel, G., Bengio, Y., Malkin, N., Tong, A. (2024). Iterated Denoising Energy Matching for Sampling from Boltzmann Densities. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 760--786. arXiv:2402.06121 uses:

∇log⁡pt(xt)≈∇xtlog⁡∑m=1Mexp⁡ ⁣(−E(xt+ϵ(m))),ϵ(m)∼N(0,σt2I)\nabla \log p_t(x_t) \approx \nabla_{x_t} \log \sum_{m=1}^{M} \exp\!\bigl(-\mathcal{E}(x_t + \epsilon^{(m)})\bigr), \qquad \epsilon^{(m)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_t^2 I)∇logpt​(xt​)≈∇xt​​logm=1∑M​exp(−E(xt​+ϵ(m))),ϵ(m)∼N(0,σt2​I)

where E\mathcal{E}E is the energy function (πT∝e−E\pi_T \propto e^{-\mathcal{E}}πT​∝e−E). This is a self-normalized importance sampling estimate: the Gaussian samples xt+ϵ(m)x_t + \epsilon^{(m)}xt​+ϵ(m) serve as proposals, and the unnormalized target e−Ee^{-\mathcal{E}}e−E provides the importance weights. The normalizing constant ZZZ cancels because it appears in both numerator and denominator. The gradient passes through the reparameterized samples via the log-sum-exp, so no score network is needed for the target itself. The network then regresses against this Monte Carlo estimate. This is a data-free analog of denoising score matching: instead of using known clean-noisy pairs (x0,xt)(x_0, x_t)(x0​,xt​), iDEM replaces the clean data with importance-weighted samples from the target energy. It is simulation-free during training (no SDE integration), though the outer loop uses the learned sampler to populate a replay buffer.

Process × objective = method

A complete neural sampler is defined by choosing a sampling process from §2.2 and a training objective from above.
