2.4 Practical tricks and perspectives

The theoretical framework above leaves many practical choices open. This section surveys the tricks that make neural samplers work (or fail) in practice.

Langevin preconditioning

He et al. [2]He, J., Du, Y., Vargas, F., Zhang, D., Padhy, S., OuYang, R., Gomes, C., Hernandez-Lobato, J. M. (2025). No Trick, No Treat: Pursuits and Challenges Towards Simulation-free Training of Neural Samplers. arXiv:2502.06685 found that the network parameterization matters more than the loss function. The key insight is Langevin preconditioning: initializing the network so that the drift starts near ∇log⁡πT\nabla \log \pi_T∇logπT​, i.e., the model behaves like Langevin dynamics toward the target at the beginning of training. Without this initialization, the network must discover the target gradient structure from scratch, and in practice simulation-free training fails regardless of loss function.

For time-reversal methods, Langevin preconditioning must be added explicitly through the network architecture (e.g., a skip connection that incorporates ∇log⁡πT\nabla \log \pi_T∇logπT​). For escorted transport, it is built in via the σt2∇log⁡πt\sigma_t^2 \nabla \log \pi_tσt2​∇logπt​ term in the SDE.

REINFORCE vs reparameterization

Two gradient estimation strategies are available:

REINFORCE (score function estimator). Treat the trajectory as a sample from the current policy and use ∇θL=E[R⋅∇θlog⁡pθ(trajectory)]\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}[R \cdot \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\text{trajectory})]∇θ​L=E[R⋅∇θ​logpθ​(trajectory)]. This does not require backprop through the SDE solver (the trajectory can be sampled with a black-box integrator), but the gradient has high variance. The LV and TB losses naturally use this approach because their gradients factor as REINFORCE-like estimators with built-in control variates [18, 22]Richter, L., Berner, J. (2024). Improved Sampling via Learned Diffusions. ICLR. arXiv:2307.01198

Richter, L., Boustati, A., Nusken, N., Ruiz, F., Akyildiz, O. D. (2020). VarGrad: A Low-Variance Gradient Estimator for Variational Inference. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33..

Reparameterization trick. Write the SDE trajectory as a deterministic function of the noise: Xn+1=Xn+μθ(Xn,tn)Δt+σnΔt ξnX_{n+1} = X_n + \mu_\theta(X_n, t_n)\Delta t + \sigma_n \sqrt{\Delta t}\,\xi_nXn+1​=Xn​+μθ​(Xn​,tn​)Δt+σn​Δt​ξn​ where ξn∼N(0,I)\xi_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)ξn​∼N(0,I). Then backpropagate through the entire chain to get ∇θL\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}∇θ​L. This gives low-variance gradients but requires storing the full computation graph (memory scales with trajectory length) and can be numerically unstable for long trajectories. Used by PIS [10]Zhang, Q., Chen, Y. (2022). Path Integral Sampler: A Stochastic Control Approach for Sampling. ICLR. arXiv:2111.15141 and DIS [8]Berner, J., Richter, L., Ullrich, K. (2024). An Optimal Control Perspective on Diffusion-Based Generative Modeling. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2211.01364 for the KL objective.

In practice, REINFORCE-based methods (TB, LV) tend to be more stable and support off-policy training, while reparameterization-based methods (KL) can be faster when the trajectory is short but become impractical for long diffusion chains.

The reparameterization trick was popularized by Kingma & Welling [26]Kingma, D. P., Welling, M. (2014). Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes. ICLR. arXiv:1312.6114 for training variational autoencoders. Its application to SDE trajectories (the “deep reparameterization trick”) was introduced by Zhang & Chen [10]Zhang, Q., Chen, Y. (2022). Path Integral Sampler: A Stochastic Control Approach for Sampling. ICLR. arXiv:2111.15141 for PIS. The REINFORCE estimator comes from policy gradient reinforcement learning (RL) [27]Williams, R. J. (1992). Simple Statistical Gradient-Following Algorithms for Connectionist Reinforcement Learning. Machine Learning, 8, 229--256.. Off-policy training with replay buffers, used with TB/LV losses, borrows directly from deep RL [28]Mnih, V., Kavukcuoglu, K., Silver, D., Rusu, A. A., Veness, J., Bellemare, M. G., Graves, A., Riedmiller, M., Fidjeland, A. K., Ostrovski, G., Petersen, S., Beattie, C., Sadik, A., Antonoglou, I., King, H., Kumaran, D., Wierstra, D., Legg, S., Hassabis, D. (2015). Human-Level Control Through Deep Reinforcement Learning. Nature, 518, 529--533.. The choice between these gradient estimators mirrors the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in RL.

On-policy vs off-policy training

On-policy means the trajectories used to estimate the gradient are sampled from the current policy P^θ\hat{\mathbb{P}}_\thetaP^θ​. This is required for the reparameterization trick (KL objective) because the gradient depends on the specific noise realization. The downside is that every gradient step requires fresh simulation.

Off-policy means the trajectories can come from a different distribution W^\hat{\mathbb{W}}W^, such as a replay buffer of previously generated trajectories, or a mixture of the current policy with an exploration distribution. The TB and LV losses support this because they are defined with respect to an arbitrary reference measure W^\hat{\mathbb{W}}W^. Off-policy training enables:

  • Replay buffers. Store previously generated trajectories and reuse them for multiple gradient steps, amortizing the cost of simulation. This is the RL-style “experience replay” trick.
  • Exploration. Mix in trajectories from a broader distribution (e.g. higher temperature) to discover modes the current policy has not found.
  • Prioritized replay. Weight stored trajectories by their log-RND magnitude to focus training on the most informative samples.

DGFS [25]Zhang, D., Chen, R. T. Q., Liu, C., Courville, A., Bengio, Y. (2024). Diffusion Generative Flow Samplers: Improving Learning Signals Through Partial Trajectory Optimization. ICLR. arXiv:2310.02679 and the local search technique of Kim et al. [29]Kim, M., Yun, T., Bengio, E., Zhang, D., Bengio, Y., Ahn, S., Park, J. (2024). Local Search GFlowNets. arXiv:2310.02710 both exploit off-policy training with replay buffers to achieve competitive results with fewer energy evaluations.

The HJB equation

The Schrödinger bridge / SOC equivalence mentioned in §2.2 has a concrete PDE formulation. In the convention used in this post, where the SDE noise is 2σ(t)dWt\sqrt{2}\sigma(t)dW_t2​σ(t)dWt​, the value function satisfies an HJB equation of the form:

∂tV+μ⃗→⋅∇V+σ2ΔV−σ2∥∇V∥2=0,V(x,T)=−log⁡πT(x)\partial_t V + \vec\mu_\rightarrow \cdot \nabla V + \sigma^2\Delta V - \sigma^2\|\nabla V\|^2 = 0, \qquad V(x, T) = -\log \pi_T(x)∂t​V+μ​→​⋅∇V+σ2ΔV−σ2∥∇V∥2=0,V(x,T)=−logπT​(x)

where V(x,t)V(x,t)V(x,t) is the value function and the optimal control is proportional to −∇V-\nabla V−∇V (the exact coefficient depends on the SDE convention). Denoising Diffusion Sampler (DDS) [7]Vargas, F., Grathwohl, W., Doucet, A. (2023). Denoising Diffusion Samplers. ICLR. arXiv:2302.13834 and Diffusion Importance Sampler (DIS) [8]Berner, J., Richter, L., Ullrich, K. (2024). An Optimal Control Perspective on Diffusion-Based Generative Modeling. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2211.01364 derive related losses from this control view. The SB perspective also connects to the Jarzynski equality and Crooks fluctuation theorem from statistical physics, which CMCD [12]Vargas, F., Padhy, S., Blessing, D., Nusken, N. (2024). Transport Meets Variational Inference: Controlled Monte Carlo Diffusions. ICLR. arXiv:2307.01050 exploits.

SMC resampling

Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) can be layered on top of many neural samplers. The idea is to run KKK parallel trajectories, compute importance weights at intermediate time steps, and resample (duplicate high-weight trajectories, discard low-weight ones). This can correct for errors in the learned drift without retraining. SMC resampling is particularly useful at inference time: train the neural SDE once, then run SMC with the learned drift as the proposal to obtain consistent weighted estimates as the particle count grows. The Particle Denoising Diffusion Sampler (PDDS) [30]Phillips, A., Dau, H., Hutchinson, M. J., De Bortoli, V., Deligiannidis, G., Doucet, A. (2024). Particle Denoising Diffusion Sampler. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 40688--40724. arXiv:2402.06320 combines DDS with SMC resampling and achieves significant improvements on challenging benchmarks.

Choice of reference process

The reference process determines the “noise schedule” of the sampler. The choice matters:

  • The variance-preserving SDE (VP-SDE) is the most common. It is ergodic and has a well-understood noise schedule. But the OU drift −βtx-\beta_t x−βt​x can fight against the learned control, especially early in training.
  • Pinned Brownian motion (PBM) pins the terminal state to zero, which is natural for problems where the prior is a point mass. But it is non-ergodic, so it offers less opportunity for global mixing than an OU reference.
  • The variance-exploding SDE (VE-SDE) is the simplest because it has no drift, but it requires more diffusion steps because there is no mean-reversion to help the process converge.
  • Prescribing marginals through escorted transport avoids the reference process entirely and instead specifies the path of intermediate distributions. This is more flexible but requires knowing ∇log⁡πt\nabla \log \pi_t∇logπt​ analytically.

2.5 Case studies

The process-and-objective framework may feel abstract. Two case studies illustrate how concrete methods instantiate it.

Case study 1: Denoising Diffusion Sampler (DDS)

Denoising Diffusion Sampler (DDS) [7]Vargas, F., Grathwohl, W., Doucet, A. (2023). Denoising Diffusion Samplers. ICLR. arXiv:2302.13834 was one of the first methods to combine time-reversal diffusion with data-free path-space training. It uses a VP-SDE reference process:

dYt=−βtYt dt+v2βt dWt,Y0∼πTdY_t = -\beta_t Y_t\,dt + v\sqrt{2\beta_t}\,dW_t, \qquad Y_0 \sim \pi_TdYt​=−βt​Yt​dt+v2βt​​dWt​,Y0​∼πT​

This Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process drives any initial sample toward N(0,v2I)\mathcal{N}(0, v^2 I)N(0,v2I). Applying Anderson’s theorem yields the forward (generative) SDE:

dXt=[βT−tXt+2v2βT−t bθ(Xt,t)] dt+v2βT−t dWt,X0∼N(0,v2I)dX_t = \bigl[\beta_{T-t} X_t + 2v^2\beta_{T-t}\,b_\theta(X_t, t)\bigr]\,dt + v\sqrt{2\beta_{T-t}}\,dW_t, \qquad X_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, v^2 I)dXt​=[βT−t​Xt​+2v2βT−t​bθ​(Xt​,t)]dt+v2βT−t​​dWt​,X0​∼N(0,v2I)

where bθ≈∇log⁡pT−tb_\theta \approx \nabla \log p_{T-t}bθ​≈∇logpT−t​ is the learned score. In practice, the SDE is discretized via Euler-Maruyama into NNN steps. At each step the forward and backward transition densities are Gaussian, so the log-RND (§2.3) can be computed in closed form:

R(X^)=log⁡pprior(X^0)ptarget(X^N)+∑n=0N−1log⁡π→,n(X^n+1∣X^n)π←,n+1(X^n∣X^n+1)R(\hat{X}) = \log \frac{p_{\text{prior}}(\hat{X}_0)}{p_{\text{target}}(\hat{X}_N)} + \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \log \frac{\pi_{\rightarrow,n}(\hat{X}_{n+1}\mid \hat{X}_n)}{\pi_{\leftarrow,n+1}(\hat{X}_n \mid \hat{X}_{n+1})}R(X^)=logptarget​(X^N​)pprior​(X^0​)​+n=0∑N−1​logπ←,n+1​(X^n​∣X^n+1​)π→,n​(X^n+1​∣X^n​)​

DDS then minimizes the reverse KL L=EP^[R]\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathbb{P}}}[R]L=EP^​[R] via the reparameterization trick (backprop through the SDE solver). Alternatively, the log-variance loss can be used for more mode-covering behavior. What makes DDS distinctive is that no target samples are needed. The score bθb_\thetabθ​ is trained purely from the path-space objective and evaluations of the unnormalized target density πT\pi_TπT​.

Case study 2: Diffusion Path Samplers via SMC (DPSMC)

Diffusion Path Samplers via SMC (DPSMC) [31]Young, J. M., Cordero-Encinar, P., Reich, S., Duncan, A., Akyildiz, O. D. (2026). Diffusion Path Samplers via Sequential Monte Carlo. arXiv:2601.21951 demonstrates that the diffusion path framework from §2.2 is powerful even without neural networks. Instead of learning the score with a network, DPSMC estimates it on the fly using Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC).

The starting point is the same as escorted transport: define a diffusion path of intermediate densities μt\mu_tμt​ that interpolate between a tractable prior and the target. Specifically, μt\mu_tμt​ is the convolution of the target with Gaussian noise of variance decreasing over time, the same family of smoothed distributions used in score-based generative modeling. The sampling SDE is:

dXt=∇log⁡μ^t(Xt) dt+2 dWtdX_t = \nabla \log \hat\mu_t(X_t)\,dt + \sqrt{2}\,dW_tdXt​=∇logμ^​t​(Xt​)dt+2​dWt​

The challenge is that ∇log⁡μt\nabla \log \mu_t∇logμt​ is intractable because it requires marginalizing over the target. Rather than learning a neural approximation, DPSMC uses SMC to estimate this score at each time step. Auxiliary variables from the smoothing distribution ϱt,x\varrho_{t,x}ϱt,x​ are propagated via MALA kernels, providing Monte Carlo score estimates. Here μ^t\hat\mu_tμ^​t​ in the SDE denotes the SMC estimate of the intractable μt\mu_tμt​.

Denoising score identity (DSI) and target score identity (TSI). The intractable score ∇log⁡μt\nabla \log \mu_t∇logμt​ can be expressed in two equivalent ways: (1) as an expectation under the posterior of the clean data given the noisy observation (DSI), or (2) as an expectation involving ∇log⁡πT\nabla \log \pi_T∇logπT​ directly (TSI). DPSMC uses an optimal linear combination of both estimators, with weights chosen to minimize variance. This is reminiscent of control variates.

DPSMC is a training-free sampler: it requires no gradient updates or learned parameters. It uses the same broad ingredients as escorted transport (§2.2), namely diffusion paths and score-guided dynamics, but replaces learned score models with classical SMC estimation. This makes it a useful reference point: it shows how far the diffusion-path idea can go without the additional power, cost, and failure modes of neural network training.

2.6 The reality check

Systematic benchmarking [2]He, J., Du, Y., Vargas, F., Zhang, D., Padhy, S., OuYang, R., Gomes, C., Hernandez-Lobato, J. M. (2025). No Trick, No Treat: Pursuits and Challenges Towards Simulation-free Training of Neural Samplers. arXiv:2502.06685 of all these methods found three sobering results:

  1. In their experiments, simulation-free training usually fails without Langevin preconditioning, regardless of loss function. The PINN loss is a partial exception but is sensitive to prior and interpolation choices.
  2. Classical Parallel Tempering MCMC combined with a post-hoc generative model beats the neural samplers in their benchmark, with far fewer energy evaluations.
  3. Since Langevin preconditioning amounts to running MCMC during training, “data-free” neural samplers may not actually be more efficient than MCMC plus fitting.

The most promising direction is probably hybridizing neural and classical approaches: use MCMC for exploration and neural networks for amortized generation.

A large-scale benchmark by Blessing et al. [21]Blessing, D., Jia, X., Esslinger, J., Vargas, F., Neumann, G. (2024). Beyond ELBOs: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Variational Methods for Sampling. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 4205--4229. arXiv:2406.07423 comparing 17 sampling methods across synthetic and Bayesian targets reinforces these findings. Key observations: mode collapse worsens dramatically in high dimensions, with methods that work in 2D failing at d=50d=50d=50 [21]Blessing, D., Jia, X., Esslinger, J., Vargas, F., Neumann, G. (2024). Beyond ELBOs: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Variational Methods for Sampling. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 4205--4229. arXiv:2406.07423; the ELBO is insensitive to missing modes (MFVI achieves good ELBO despite severe mode collapse); no single method dominates across all tasks; and, within the tested diffusion-style methods, using more diffusion steps often improves performance. They also find that resampling in SMC can cause mode collapse in high dimensions, and that learning the initial distribution π0\pi_0π0​ end-to-end often leads to mode collapse.

3. Non-differentiable targets

When the state space is discrete, say x∈{−1,+1}Nx \in \{-1,+1\}^Nx∈{−1,+1}N or x∈{0,1}Nx \in \{0,1\}^Nx∈{0,1}N, the ordinary gradient ∇xlog⁡π(x)\nabla_x \log \pi(x)∇x​logπ(x) is not defined. Langevin dynamics therefore cannot be applied directly. Classical methods (Metropolis-Hastings, cluster algorithms, Parallel Tempering) work with energy evaluations and local or collective moves, but they can mix slowly and produce highly correlated samples. Deep learning offers several alternatives: autoregressive models (VAN), flow networks (GFlowNet), discrete diffusion (DiffUCO), and discrete Schrödinger bridge samplers (DASBS). We begin with the classical toolkit (§3.1) before surveying these neural approaches.

Figure 6. Ising model (16×16) using Metropolis single-spin-flip dynamics. Drag the slider to change inverse temperature β\betaβ. The same spin configuration evolves as you adjust β\betaβ, running 200 Metropolis sweeps per update. Low β\betaβ gives disordered spins; high β\betaβ produces ordered domains.

The Ising model assigns probability pβ(x)∝exp⁡(β∑(i,j)∈EJij xixj+β∑ihi xi)p_\beta(x) \propto \exp(\beta \sum_{(i,j)\in E} J_{ij}\,x_i x_j + \beta \sum_i h_i\,x_i)pβ​(x)∝exp(β∑(i,j)∈E​Jij​xi​xj​+β∑i​hi​xi​) to spin configurations. This is the Boltzmann form e−βH(x)e^{-\beta H(x)}e−βH(x) with energy H(x)=−∑Jij xixj−∑hi xiH(x) = -\sum J_{ij}\,x_i x_j - \sum h_i\,x_iH(x)=−∑Jij​xi​xj​−∑hi​xi​ (the sign convention absorbs the minus into HHH so that low energy means aligned spins). At high β\betaβ, energy barriers are steep and local spin-flip samplers mix very slowly.

3.1 Classical methods

Before turning to neural approaches, we survey the classical toolkit for sampling from discrete distributions with intractable normalizing constants. These methods predate deep learning by decades and remain practical workhorses in many applications. They also set the baseline that any neural method must beat.

Metropolis-Hastings with local moves

The Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm from §2.1 applies directly to discrete spaces. The only change is the proposal distribution. For binary variables x∈{−1,+1}Nx \in \{-1,+1\}^Nx∈{−1,+1}N, the simplest proposal is a single spin flip: pick a site iii uniformly at random and propose x′x'x′ that differs from xxx only at site iii. The acceptance probability is:

A(x′∣x)=min⁡ ⁣(1,  π(x′)π(x))A(x'\mid x) = \min\!\left(1,\;\frac{\pi(x')}{\pi(x)}\right)A(x′∣x)=min(1,π(x)π(x′)​)

where the proposal ratio q(x∣x′)/q(x′∣x)=1q(x\mid x')/q(x'\mid x) = 1q(x∣x′)/q(x′∣x)=1 cancels because the proposal is symmetric. For the Ising model, the energy difference ΔE=E(x′)−E(x)\Delta E = E(x') - E(x)ΔE=E(x′)−E(x) depends only on the flipped spin and its neighbors, so each step costs O(degree)O(\text{degree})O(degree) rather than O(N)O(N)O(N). This locality is a major practical advantage.

The Gibbs sampler is a special case: instead of proposing and accepting/rejecting, resample site iii directly from its conditional distribution p(xi∣x−i)p(x_i \mid x_{-i})p(xi​∣x−i​). For the Ising model, this conditional is a single sigmoid, so every update is accepted. Gibbs sampling is equivalent to MH with a particular proposal and acceptance probability of 1, but it requires tractable conditional distributions.

Both methods satisfy detailed balance and converge to the target distribution. The problem is speed. Near a phase transition (e.g. the Ising model at β≈βc\beta \approx \beta_cβ≈βc​), the system develops long-range correlations and the mixing time can grow as a power law in NNN (critical slowing down). In the ordered phase (β>βc\beta > \beta_cβ>βc​, i.e. below the critical temperature), metastable states (e.g. the two magnetization phases of the Ising model) create energy barriers that single-spin-flip dynamics cross only after exponentially many steps.

Cluster algorithms: Swendsen-Wang and Wolff

Cluster algorithms were designed specifically to overcome critical slowing down in spin systems. Instead of flipping one spin at a time, they identify and flip entire clusters of correlated spins in a single move.

The Swendsen-Wang algorithm [32]Swendsen, R. H., Wang, J. (1987). Nonuniversal Critical Dynamics in Monte Carlo Simulations. Physical Review Letters, 58, 86--88. works as follows for a ferromagnetic Ising model without external fields. For each edge (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) where xi=xjx_i = x_jxi​=xj​, place a bond with probability 1−e−2βJij1 - e^{-2\beta J_{ij}}1−e−2βJij​. The bonded sites form clusters. Independently assign each cluster a new spin value ±1\pm 1±1 with equal probability. This is one sweep. The key insight is that the bond probability is chosen so that the joint distribution over spins and bonds satisfies detailed balance with respect to the Ising target. Because entire clusters flip together, the algorithm can rearrange large regions of the configuration in a single step.

The Wolff algorithm [33]Wolff, U. (1989). Collective Monte Carlo Updating for Spin Systems. Physical Review Letters, 62, 361--364. is a single-cluster variant: pick a random seed spin, grow a cluster by adding aligned neighbors with the same bond probability, and flip the entire cluster. Wolff is often preferred in practice because it automatically adapts the cluster size to the correlation length: near criticality, clusters grow large, which is exactly when large moves are needed.

Why cluster algorithms work. The bond probability 1−e−2βJ1 - e^{-2\beta J}1−e−2βJ is not arbitrary. It comes from the Fortuin-Kasteleyn representation of the Ising/Potts model, which maps the spin system to a random cluster (percolation) model. In this representation, the cluster updates are exact: they satisfy detailed balance without any accept/reject step. At the critical point, the clusters are fractal and span the system, so a single Wolff step can decorrelate the entire configuration. This reduces the dynamic critical exponent zzz from ≈2\approx 2≈2 (local dynamics) to ≈0.25\approx 0.25≈0.25 for the 2D Ising model.

The limitation is generality. Cluster algorithms exploit the specific algebraic structure of ferromagnetic Ising and Potts models through the FK representation. They do not extend straightforwardly to arbitrary energy functions, frustrated systems, external fields, or non-pairwise interactions. For general discrete distributions, we need other strategies.

Simulated annealing and parallel tempering

Simulated annealing [34]Kirkpatrick, S., Gelatt, Jr., C. Daniel, Vecchi, M. P. (1983). Optimization by Simulated Annealing. Science, 220, 671--680. is the discrete analog of the annealing idea from §2.1. Start at high temperature (β\betaβ small), where the energy landscape is smooth and the sampler mixes freely. Gradually lower the temperature (β→βtarget\beta \to \beta_{\text{target}}β→βtarget​), allowing the system to settle into low-energy configurations. The cooling schedule determines the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation. With sufficiently slow logarithmic cooling, simulated annealing can be guaranteed to converge to a global minimum. In practice, faster schedules are used and the result is approximate.

Simulated annealing is an optimization algorithm, not a sampler: it produces a single low-energy configuration, not samples from the Boltzmann distribution. To get samples, we need parallel tempering, also called replica exchange MCMC [35, 36]Swendsen, R. H., Wang, J. (1986). Replica Monte Carlo Simulation of Spin-Glasses. Physical Review Letters, 57, 2607--2609.

Geyer, C. J. (1991). Markov Chain Monte Carlo Maximum Likelihood. Computing Science and Statistics: Proceedings of the 23rd Symposium on the Interface.. The idea is to run multiple replicas of the system simultaneously at different temperatures β1<β2<⋯<βK\beta_1 < \beta_2 < \cdots < \beta_Kβ1​<β2​<⋯<βK​, where βK=βtarget\beta_K = \beta_{\text{target}}βK​=βtarget​. Each replica runs its own MCMC chain (e.g. single-spin-flip MH). Periodically, adjacent replicas propose to swap their configurations. The swap between replicas at temperatures βi\beta_iβi​ and βj\beta_jβj​ with configurations xix_ixi​ and xjx_jxj​ is accepted with probability:

Aswap=min⁡ ⁣(1,  exp⁡[(βi−βj)(E(xi)−E(xj))])A_{\text{swap}} = \min\!\left(1,\;\exp\bigl[(\beta_i - \beta_j)(E(x_i) - E(x_j))\bigr]\right)Aswap​=min(1,exp[(βi​−βj​)(E(xi​)−E(xj​))])

This satisfies detailed balance for the joint distribution over all replicas. The high-temperature replicas explore freely and discover new modes; the swap moves propagate this information down to the target temperature. Parallel tempering is the most robust general-purpose method for multimodal discrete distributions and is the classical baseline that neural methods must beat.

Parallel tempering as a baseline. The benchmarking results of He et al. [2]He, J., Du, Y., Vargas, F., Zhang, D., Padhy, S., OuYang, R., Gomes, C., Hernandez-Lobato, J. M. (2025). No Trick, No Treat: Pursuits and Challenges Towards Simulation-free Training of Neural Samplers. arXiv:2502.06685 in the continuous setting found that parallel tempering MCMC combined with a post-hoc generative model outperformed neural samplers. The same lesson applies in discrete settings: parallel tempering is simple, requires no training, and handles multimodality through temperature swaps rather than learned transport. Any neural discrete sampler should be compared against a well-tuned parallel tempering baseline.

From classical to neural discrete samplers

The classical methods above share a common limitation: they generate samples sequentially, with each new sample correlated with the previous one. Thinning (keeping every kkk-th sample) reduces correlation but wastes computation. The autocorrelation time, the number of steps needed for an effectively independent sample, can be enormous for hard problems.

Neural methods (§3.2–§3.6) aim to break this bottleneck by learning a generative model that produces independent samples in a single forward pass (VAN, GFlowNet) or a short diffusion chain (DiffUCO, DASBS). The tradeoff is training cost: learning the generative model requires many energy evaluations upfront, but once trained, sampling is fast and embarrassingly parallel. Whether this amortization pays off depends on how many samples are needed and how expensive the energy function is to evaluate.

3.2 Variational Autoregressive Networks (VAN)

In §2 we saw that continuous diffusion samplers learn a stochastic process that transports a prior to the target, trained by minimizing a divergence on path space. Variational Autoregressive Networks (VAN) [37]Wu, D., Wang, L., Zhang, P. (2019). Solving Statistical Mechanics Using Variational Autoregressive Networks. Physical Review Letters, 122, 080602. arXiv:1809.10606 solve the same problem in discrete space using a completely different strategy: they directly parameterize a tractable approximation qθq_\thetaqθ​ to the target pβp_\betapβ​, without any diffusion process at all.

The autoregressive factorization

Any joint distribution over NNN binary variables can be written exactly as a product of conditionals (the chain rule of probability):

qθ(s)=∏i=1Nqθ(si∣s1,…,si−1)q_\theta(s) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} q_\theta(s_i \mid s_1, \ldots, s_{i-1})qθ​(s)=i=1∏N​qθ​(si​∣s1​,…,si−1​)

Each conditional qθ(si∣s<i)q_\theta(s_i \mid s_{< i})qθ​(si​∣s<i​) is a Bernoulli distribution: qθ(si=+1∣s<i)=σ(NNθ(s<i,i))q_\theta(s_i = +1 \mid s_{< i}) = \sigma(\text{NN}_\theta(s_{< i}, i))qθ​(si​=+1∣s<i​)=σ(NNθ​(s<i​,i)) where σ\sigmaσ is the sigmoid function. This factorization is exact and gives two things for free. First, direct sampling: draw s1∼qθ(s1)s_1 \sim q_\theta(s_1)s1​∼qθ​(s1​), then s2∼qθ(s2∣s1)s_2 \sim q_\theta(s_2 \mid s_1)s2​∼qθ​(s2​∣s1​), and so on. Second, exact log-likelihood: log⁡qθ(s)=∑i=1Nlog⁡qθ(si∣s<i)\log q_\theta(s) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log q_\theta(s_i \mid s_{< i})logqθ​(s)=∑i=1N​logqθ​(si​∣s<i​).

The original architecture is MADE [38]Germain, M., Gregor, K., Murray, I., Larochelle, H. (2015). MADE: Masked Autoencoder for Distribution Estimation. Proceedings of the 32nd International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 37, 881--889. arXiv:1502.03509 (Masked Autoencoder for Distribution Estimation), a feed-forward network with binary masks on the weight matrices that enforce the autoregressive property in a single forward pass. Later work uses RNNs [39]Hibat-Allah, M., Inack, E. M., Wiersema, R., Melko, R. G., Carrasquilla, J. (2021). Variational Neural Annealing. Nature Machine Intelligence, 3, 952--961., GNNs, or transformers.

Training objective

We want qθ≈pβq_\theta \approx p_\betaqθ​≈pβ​ where pβ(s)=e−βE(s)/Zp_\beta(s) = e^{-\beta E(s)}/Zpβ​(s)=e−βE(s)/Z. The training objective is the variational free energy:

Fq=Es∼qθ ⁣[E(s)+1βlog⁡qθ(s)]=⟨E⟩qθ−1βH(qθ)F_q = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim q_\theta}\!\left[E(s) + \frac{1}{\beta}\log q_\theta(s)\right] = \langle E \rangle_{q_\theta} - \frac{1}{\beta}H(q_\theta)Fq​=Es∼qθ​​[E(s)+β1​logqθ​(s)]=⟨E⟩qθ​​−β1​H(qθ​)

To see why this works, we insert ±1βlog⁡Z\pm \frac{1}{\beta}\log Z±β1​logZ inside the expectation to recognize a KL divergence:

Fq=Es∼qθ ⁣[1βlog⁡qθ(s)−1βlog⁡e−βE(s)Z]−1βlog⁡Z=1β DKL(qθ∥pβ)+F,F=−1βlog⁡ZF_q = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim q_\theta}\!\left[\frac{1}{\beta}\log q_\theta(s) - \frac{1}{\beta}\log \frac{e^{-\beta E(s)}}{Z}\right] - \frac{1}{\beta}\log Z = \frac{1}{\beta}\,D_{\text{KL}}(q_\theta \| p_\beta) + F, \qquad F = -\frac{1}{\beta}\log ZFq​=Es∼qθ​​[β1​logqθ​(s)−β1​logZe−βE(s)​]−β1​logZ=β1​DKL​(qθ​∥pβ​)+F,F=−β1​logZ

The key step is recognizing that E(s)+1βlog⁡qθ(s)=1β[log⁡qθ(s)−log⁡(e−βE(s)/Z)]−1βlog⁡Z=1βlog⁡qθ(s)pβ(s)+FE(s) + \frac{1}{\beta}\log q_\theta(s) = \frac{1}{\beta}[\log q_\theta(s) - \log(e^{-\beta E(s)}/Z)] - \frac{1}{\beta}\log Z = \frac{1}{\beta}\log \frac{q_\theta(s)}{p_\beta(s)} + FE(s)+β1​logqθ​(s)=β1​[logqθ​(s)−log(e−βE(s)/Z)]−β1​logZ=β1​logpβ​(s)qθ​(s)​+F, which is exactly the KL divergence plus a constant.

Since FFF is constant, minimizing FqF_qFq​ is equivalent to minimizing the reverse KL to the Boltzmann distribution. This is the same reverse KL that appears in the continuous-time path-space objectives of §2.3, but applied to a single-step model rather than a multi-step trajectory.

The gradient is estimated via REINFORCE:

∇θFq=Es∼qθ ⁣[(E(s)+1βlog⁡qθ(s)−b) ∇θlog⁡qθ(s)]\nabla_\theta F_q = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim q_\theta}\!\left[\bigl(E(s) + \tfrac{1}{\beta}\log q_\theta(s) - b\bigr)\,\nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(s)\right]∇θ​Fq​=Es∼qθ​​[(E(s)+β1​logqθ​(s)−b)∇θ​logqθ​(s)]

where bbb is a variance-reduction baseline (e.g. running mean). This is the same REINFORCE estimator used in policy gradient RL. The connection is not a coincidence: VAN [37]Wu, D., Wang, L., Zhang, P. (2019). Solving Statistical Mechanics Using Variational Autoregressive Networks. Physical Review Letters, 122, 080602. arXiv:1809.10606 is essentially a one-step RL agent whose “policy” is qθq_\thetaqθ​ and whose “reward” is −βE(s)-\beta E(s)−βE(s).

Unlike mean-field approximations (which assume q(s)=∏iq(si)q(s) = \prod_i q(s_i)q(s)=∏i​q(si​) and cannot capture correlations), the autoregressive factorization can represent any distribution. The main limitation is the sequential bottleneck: generating one sample requires NNN sequential network evaluations.

3.3 Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets)

VAN [37]Wu, D., Wang, L., Zhang, P. (2019). Solving Statistical Mechanics Using Variational Autoregressive Networks. Physical Review Letters, 122, 080602. arXiv:1809.10606 fixes a generation order (s1,s2,…,sNs_1, s_2, \ldots, s_Ns1​,s2​,…,sN​) and learns the conditionals. But for many combinatorial objects, there is no natural ordering, and different orderings may make the problem easier or harder. Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) [40, 41]Bengio, E., Jain, M., Korablyov, M., Precup, D., Bengio, Y. (2021). Flow Network Based Generative Models for Non-Iterative Diverse Candidate Generation. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems Curran Associates, Inc., 34, 27381--27394. arXiv:2106.04399

Bengio, Y., Lahlou, S., Deleu, T., Hu, E. J., Tiwari, M., Bengio, E. (2023). GFlowNet Foundations. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 24, 1--55. arXiv:2111.09266 remove this constraint by learning a stochastic policy over a DAG where multiple construction orders can produce the same object.

The DAG and trajectories

The construction process is defined on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with a distinguished initial state. States S\mathcal{S}S are partially constructed objects (e.g. partial bit strings). There is an initial state s0s_0s0​ (the empty object), terminal states X\mathcal{X}X (fully constructed objects), and a special sink state sfs_fsf​. Edges s→s′s \to s's→s′ are construction steps (e.g. “set bit 2 to 1”). A complete trajectory τ=(s0→s1→⋯→sn→sf)\tau = (s_0 \to s_1 \to \cdots \to s_n \to s_f)τ=(s0​→s1​→⋯→sn​→sf​) builds an object x=snx = s_nx=sn​ step by step. The key property is that multiple trajectories can reach the same terminal state.

Flows and the sampling distribution

A flow function FFF assigns a non-negative number to each edge, satisfying flow conservation at every intermediate state:

∑s′∈Par(s)F(s′→s)=∑s′′∈Child(s)F(s→s′′)=F(s)\sum_{s' \in \text{Par}(s)} F(s' \to s) = \sum_{s'' \in \text{Child}(s)} F(s \to s'') = F(s)s′∈Par(s)∑​F(s′→s)=s′′∈Child(s)∑​F(s→s′′)=F(s)

The forward policy samples the next state proportionally to edge flow:

PF(s′∣s)=F(s→s′)F(s)P_F(s' \mid s) = \frac{F(s \to s')}{F(s)}PF​(s′∣s)=F(s)F(s→s′)​

If the terminating flow matches the reward, F(x→sf)=R(x)F(x \to s_f) = R(x)F(x→sf​)=R(x), then the probability of generating any object xxx is:

PT(x)=R(x)Z,Z=F(s0)=∑x∈XR(x)P_T(x) = \frac{R(x)}{Z}, \qquad Z = F(s_0) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} R(x)PT​(x)=ZR(x)​,Z=F(s0​)=x∈X∑​R(x)

For Boltzmann sampling, set R(x)=e−βE(x)R(x) = e^{-\beta E(x)}R(x)=e−βE(x).

Training objectives

The goal is not to find a single best object, but to sample objects in proportion to their reward. GFlowNet objectives enforce that by making local or trajectory-level flow equations consistent.

Three objectives enforce the flow constraints at different granularities, closely paralleling the continuous-time losses in §2.3:

Flow matching (FM) [40]Bengio, E., Jain, M., Korablyov, M., Precup, D., Bengio, Y. (2021). Flow Network Based Generative Models for Non-Iterative Diverse Candidate Generation. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems Curran Associates, Inc., 34, 27381--27394. arXiv:2106.04399 penalizes violations of flow conservation at each state. LFM(s)=(log⁡∑s′F(s′→s)−log⁡∑s′′F(s→s′′))2\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}(s) = (\log \sum_{s'} F(s' \to s) - \log \sum_{s''} F(s \to s''))^2LFM​(s)=(log∑s′​F(s′→s)−log∑s′′​F(s→s′′))2. This requires summing over all parents and children.

Detailed balance (DB) [41]Bengio, Y., Lahlou, S., Deleu, T., Hu, E. J., Tiwari, M., Bengio, E. (2023). GFlowNet Foundations. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 24, 1--55. arXiv:2111.09266 enforces balance at each edge.

F(s) PF(s′∣s)=F(s′) PB(s∣s′)F(s)\,P_F(s' \mid s) = F(s')\,P_B(s \mid s')F(s)PF​(s′∣s)=F(s′)PB​(s∣s′)

The loss is LDB(s→s′)=(log⁡F(s)+log⁡PF(s′∣s)−log⁡F(s′)−log⁡PB(s∣s′))2\mathcal{L}_{\text{DB}}(s \to s') = (\log F(s) + \log P_F(s'\mid s) - \log F(s') - \log P_B(s\mid s'))^2LDB​(s→s′)=(logF(s)+logPF​(s′∣s)−logF(s′)−logPB​(s∣s′))2. This avoids explicit sums and works in continuous state spaces. Compare with the continuous-time DB loss in §2.3: the same structure, with F(s)F(s)F(s) playing the role of p^n\hat{p}_np^​n​ and PF/PBP_F/P_BPF​/PB​ playing the role of π→/π←\pi_\rightarrow/\pi_\leftarrowπ→​/π←​.

Trajectory balance (TB) [23]Malkin, N., Jain, M., Bengio, E., Sun, C., Bengio, Y. (2022). Trajectory Balance: Improved Credit Assignment in GFlowNets. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 35, 5955--5967. arXiv:2201.13259 enforces a global constraint on complete trajectories.

Z⋅∏t=0n−1PF(st+1∣st)=R(x)⋅∏t=1nPB(st−1∣st)Z \cdot \prod_{t=0}^{n-1} P_F(s_{t+1} \mid s_t) = R(x) \cdot \prod_{t=1}^{n} P_B(s_{t-1} \mid s_t)Z⋅t=0∏n−1​PF​(st+1​∣st​)=R(x)⋅t=1∏n​PB​(st−1​∣st​)

The loss is LTB(τ)=(log⁡Z+log⁡PF(τ)−log⁡R(x)−log⁡PB(τ))2\mathcal{L}_{\text{TB}}(\tau) = (\log Z + \log P_F(\tau) - \log R(x) - \log P_B(\tau))^2LTB​(τ)=(logZ+logPF​(τ)−logR(x)−logPB​(τ))2. This has the same path-ratio structure as the continuous-time TB loss, with PF/PBP_F/P_BPF​/PB​ playing the role of π→/π←\pi_\rightarrow/\pi_\leftarrowπ→​/π←​ and R(x)/ZR(x)/ZR(x)/Z playing the role of ptarget(XT)p_{\text{target}}(X_T)ptarget​(XT​).

Berner et al. [20]Berner, J., Richter, L., Sendera, M., Rector-Brooks, J., Malkin, N. (2026). From Discrete-Time Policies to Continuous-Time Diffusion Samplers: Asymptotic Equivalences and Faster Training. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2501.06148 proved precise asymptotic links between discrete-time GFlowNet-style objectives and continuous-time path-space divergences as the discretization becomes finer. This does not make every GFlowNet literally an SDE, but it explains why the same balance and trajectory-ratio losses keep reappearing in both literatures.

GFlowNet vs RL

Standard RL maximizes expected reward, producing a deterministic policy that finds the single best object (mode-seeking). GFlowNets instead learn PT(x)∝R(x)P_T(x) \propto R(x)PT​(x)∝R(x), a stochastic, mode-covering policy. Entropy-regularized RL (MaxEnt RL) yields PT(x)∝n(x)⋅R(x)1/αP_T(x) \propto n(x) \cdot R(x)^{1/\alpha}PT​(x)∝n(x)⋅R(x)1/α where n(x)n(x)n(x) is the number of trajectories reaching xxx and α>0\alpha > 0α>0 is the entropy regularization coefficient, which is not the same as PT(x)∝R(x)P_T(x) \propto R(x)PT​(x)∝R(x) unless the DAG is a tree.

3.4 Diffusion for Unsupervised Combinatorial Optimization (DiffUCO)

Both VAN [37]Wu, D., Wang, L., Zhang, P. (2019). Solving Statistical Mechanics Using Variational Autoregressive Networks. Physical Review Letters, 122, 080602. arXiv:1809.10606 and GFlowNet have a sequential bottleneck: O(N)O(N)O(N) forward passes to generate NNN variables. DiffUCO [42]Sanokowski, S., Hochreiter, S., Lehner, S. (2024). A Diffusion Model Framework for Unsupervised Neural Combinatorial Optimization. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 43346--43367. arXiv:2406.01661 was proposed for unsupervised neural combinatorial optimization, but it is relevant here because its diffusion chain can also be interpreted as an approximate sampler or proposal distribution over low-energy configurations. It updates all bits in parallel, generating entire configurations non-autoregressively.

Backward (noising) process. A corruption process gradually destroys a target configuration into noise by flipping bits with increasing probability. This runs from t=Tt=Tt=T (target) to t=0t=0t=0 (noise), matching our convention. Unlike autoregressive models, the noising process operates on all variables simultaneously.

Forward (generative) process. The generative model predicts the next (cleaner) configuration from the current (noisier) one using a non-autoregressive mean-field parameterization:

qθ(Xt+1∣Xt)=∏i=1Nq^θ(Xt)i Xt+1,i  (1−q^θ(Xt)i)1−Xt+1,iq_\theta(X_{t+1} \mid X_t) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} \hat{q}_\theta(X_t)_i^{\,X_{t+1,i}}\;(1 - \hat{q}_\theta(X_t)_i)^{1-X_{t+1,i}}qθ​(Xt+1​∣Xt​)=i=1∏N​q^​θ​(Xt​)iXt+1,i​​(1−q^​θ​(Xt​)i​)1−Xt+1,i​

Each step is a product of independent Bernoullis. Expressivity comes from composing TTT denoising steps. A single step is mean-field, but the full chain can capture correlations.

Training uses a variational upper bound on the reverse KL:

DKL(qθ(XT)∥πT(XT))≤DKL(qθ(X0:T)∥p(X0:T))D_{\text{KL}}(q_\theta(X_T) \| \pi_T(X_T)) \leq D_{\text{KL}}(q_\theta(X_{0:T}) \| p(X_{0:T}))DKL​(qθ​(XT​)∥πT​(XT​))≤DKL​(qθ​(X0:T​)∥p(X0:T​))

The gap is Eqθ(XT)[DKL(qθ(X0:T−1∣XT)∥p(X0:T−1∣XT))]≥0\mathbb{E}_{q_\theta(X_T)}[D_{\text{KL}}(q_\theta(X_{0:T-1}\mid X_T) \| p(X_{0:T-1}\mid X_T))] \geq 0Eqθ​(XT​)​[DKL​(qθ​(X0:T−1​∣XT​)∥p(X0:T−1​∣XT​))]≥0, where p(X0:T−1∣XT)p(X_{0:T-1}\mid X_T)p(X0:T−1​∣XT​) is the backward noising process conditioned on the clean sample. More diffusion steps can make the latent chain more expressive and reduce discretization error, but they also increase compute. This is the same path-space KL structure as in §2.3, applied to discrete variables.

3.5 Discrete Schrödinger Bridge Samplers (DASBS)

The continuous-time SB framework from §2.3 has a natural discrete analog. Just as continuous diffusion samplers learn optimal SDEs to transport a prior to the target, we can learn optimal continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs) that transport a discrete prior to a discrete target. The DASBS [43]Guo, W., Zhu, Y., Du, X., Nam, J., Chen, Y., Gomez-Bombarelli, R., Liu, G., Tao, M., Choi, J. (2026). Discrete Adjoint Schrodinger Bridge Sampler. arXiv:2602.08243 develops this theory.

Continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). A CTMC is a stochastic process on a discrete state space X\mathcal{X}X characterized by transition rates rt(y,x)r_t(y,x)rt​(y,x): the probability of jumping from state xxx to state yyy in an infinitesimal time dtdtdt is rt(y,x) dtr_t(y,x)\,dtrt​(y,x)dt. CTMCs are the discrete-state analog of SDEs. The forward Kolmogorov equation ∂tpt(x)=∑y[rt(x,y) pt(y)−rt(y,x) pt(x)]\partial_t p_t(x) = \sum_y [r_t(x,y)\,p_t(y) - r_t(y,x)\,p_t(x)]∂t​pt​(x)=∑y​[rt​(x,y)pt​(y)−rt​(y,x)pt​(x)] replaces the Fokker-Planck equation.

Problem setup

Consider a discrete state space X=[N]D\mathcal{X} = [N]^DX=[N]D (e.g., DDD spins each taking NNN values). Given a reference CTMC with transition rate rt(y,x)r_t(y,x)rt​(y,x) and induced path measure prp^rpr, the discrete Schrödinger bridge problem seeks an optimal controlled rate ut(y,x)u_t(y,x)ut​(y,x) that minimizes the path-space KL divergence while matching the target marginal:

min⁡u  s.t.  p1u=νKL(pu∥pr)=EX∼pu∫01∑y≠Xt(utlog⁡utrt+rt−ut)(y,Xt) dt\min_{u \;\text{s.t.}\; p_1^u = \nu} \text{KL}(p^u \| p^r) = \mathbb{E}_{X \sim p^u} \int_0^1 \sum_{y \neq X_t} \left(u_t \log \frac{u_t}{r_t} + r_t - u_t\right)(y, X_t)\,dtus.t.p1u​=νmin​KL(pu∥pr)=EX∼pu​∫01​y=Xt​∑​(ut​logrt​ut​​+rt​−ut​)(y,Xt​)dt

This has the same structure as the continuous SB problem from §2.3, but with transition rates replacing drift controls.

Optimal transition rate

The optimal rate has an elegant form in terms of SB potentials (φt,φ^t)(\varphi_t, \hat\varphi_t)(φt​,φ^​t​):

ut∗(y,x)=φt(y)φt(x) rt(y,x),∀ y≠xu_t^*(y,x) = \frac{\varphi_t(y)}{\varphi_t(x)}\,r_t(y,x), \qquad \forall\, y \neq xut∗​(y,x)=φt​(x)φt​(y)​rt​(y,x),∀y=x

This is the discrete analog of u∗=−σ2∇Vu^* = -\sigma^2 \nabla Vu∗=−σ2∇V in continuous SOC. The potentials satisfy forward-backward equations analogous to the continuous SB potentials, with boundary conditions φ0φ^0=μ\varphi_0 \hat\varphi_0 = \muφ0​φ^​0​=μ (prior) and φ1φ^1=ν\varphi_1 \hat\varphi_1 = \nuφ1​φ^​1​=ν (target).

The stochastic optimal control (SOC) connection. Just as in the continuous case (§2.4), the discrete SB problem is equivalent to a stochastic optimal control problem with terminal cost g=log⁡φ^1νg = \log \frac{\hat\varphi_1}{\nu}g=logνφ^​1​​. This provides the same theoretical bridge between distributionally constrained optimization (SB) and unconstrained control (SOC) that underpins the continuous framework.

The cyclic group trick

The key challenge in extending adjoint matching (AM) from continuous to discrete spaces is the lack of additive noise. In continuous space, Brownian motion is additive: sampling from p1∣tr(⋅∣x)p_{1|t}^r(\cdot|x)p1∣tr​(⋅∣x) amounts to adding Gaussian noise to xxx. To recover this structure in discrete space, DASBS treats [N]D[N]^D[N]D as ZND\mathbb{Z}_N^DZND​ (the cyclic group of integers modulo NNN) and uses a uniform reference rate:

rt(y,x)=γtN,∀ y≠x  with  dH(y,x)=1r_t(y,x) = \frac{\gamma_t}{N}, \qquad \forall\, y \neq x \;\text{with}\; d_H(y,x) = 1rt​(y,x)=Nγt​​,∀y=xwithdH​(y,x)=1

where γt\gamma_tγt​ is a noise schedule and dHd_HdH​ is the Hamming distance. Under this choice, the reference transition kernel becomes additive in the group sense: sampling from p1∣tr(⋅∣x)p_{1|t}^r(\cdot|x)p1∣tr​(⋅∣x) can be written as x+ϵx + \epsilonx+ϵ where ϵ\epsilonϵ is a random element of ZND\mathbb{Z}_N^DZND​, closely paralleling the continuous case.

Controller and corrector learning

With additive noise structure recovered, DASBS learns two components via alternating optimization:

  1. Controller Φt(x)∈RD×N\Phi_t(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{D\times N}Φt​(x)∈RD×N outputs neighbor-wise ratios, with entries Φt(x)d,n≈φt(xd←n)/φt(x)\Phi_t(x)_{d,n} \approx \varphi_t(x^{d \leftarrow n})/\varphi_t(x)Φt​(x)d,n​≈φt​(xd←n)/φt​(x). These ratios determine the optimal transition rates. The controller is learned via a target-score matching objective that uses the discrete score ν(xd←n)/ν(x)\nu(x^{d \leftarrow n})/\nu(x)ν(xd←n)/ν(x), the ratio of the target distribution at neighboring states. This is the discrete analog of ∇log⁡ν\nabla \log \nu∇logν in continuous AM.

  2. Corrector Φ^(x)\hat\Phi(x)Φ^(x) approximates the boundary potential ratio φ^1(y)/φ^1(x)\hat\varphi_1(y)/\hat\varphi_1(x)φ^​1​(y)/φ^​1​(x). It is learned via adjoint matching or denoising matching, analogous to the continuous ASBS corrector.

The alternating update fixes the corrector while learning the controller, then fixes the controller while learning the corrector. This is the discrete analog of the alternating structure used in continuous ASBS and IPF-style SB solvers. The exact theory gives convergence under suitable assumptions for the idealized updates; with neural parameterizations, this should be read as a principled training scheme rather than a blanket guarantee.

Adjoint matching (AM) versus denoising matching (DM). DASBS reveals an important distinction: adjoint matching uses target-score matching, while denoising matching uses the score of the reference transition kernel. AM provides a stronger supervisory signal and faster convergence in experiments, echoing the well-known advantage of target matching over denoising matching in score estimation for continuous distributions.

DASBS achieves competitive sample quality on challenging discrete benchmarks (Ising and Potts models at phase transition) with significant training efficiency gains, demonstrating that the SB/SOC framework transfers to discrete spaces when equipped with the right algebraic structure.

3.6 Advances from discrete diffusion models

Recent progress in discrete diffusion for language modeling suggests several techniques that could strengthen the sampling-from-energy methods discussed above. DASBS (§3.5) provides a principled SB framework for discrete sampling; the techniques below offer complementary building blocks that have not yet been fully explored in this setting.

Masked diffusion models. Instead of flipping bits randomly (categorical noise), mask tokens to a special [MASK] state and learn to predict the original token. This is analogous to BERT-style denoising and has been shown to be more sample-efficient than uniform corruption in generative modeling tasks. For energy-based sampling, masking could replace the categorical noise in DiffUCO, potentially improving the quality of the learned denoising distribution. The key advantage is that masking provides a cleaner learning signal: the model only needs to predict masked positions, rather than distinguishing between corrupted and uncorrupted bits.

Continuous-time discrete diffusion (CTMC). Instead of discrete time steps, model the corruption as a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) with rate matrix QtQ_tQt​. The noising process evolves as dp/dt=Qt pdp/dt = Q_t\,pdp/dt=Qt​p and the generative (denoising) process can be derived analogously to Anderson’s theorem for continuous-state SDEs. This gives a principled way to define the “score” in discrete space as the ratio p(x′)/p(x)p(x')/p(x)p(x′)/p(x) for neighboring states x,x′x, x'x,x′, which can be learned by a neural network. Campbell et al. [44]Campbell, A., Benton, J., De Bortoli, V., Rainforth, T., Deligiannidis, G., Doucet, A. (2022). A Continuous Time Framework for Discrete Denoising Models. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems Curran Associates, Inc., 35, 28266--28279. arXiv:2205.14987 and Lou et al. [45]Lou, A., Meng, C., Ermon, S. (2024). Discrete Diffusion Modeling by Estimating the Ratios of the Data Distribution. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 32819--32848. arXiv:2310.16834 develop this theory for generative modeling; adapting it to energy-based sampling is a natural next step, and DASBS (§3.5) can be seen as one such adaptation.

Score entropy loss. In continuous space, the score matching loss avoids computing the partition function. The discrete analog, the score entropy loss introduced by Lou et al. [45]Lou, A., Meng, C., Ermon, S. (2024). Discrete Diffusion Modeling by Estimating the Ratios of the Data Distribution. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 32819--32848. arXiv:2310.16834, minimizes ∑x′q(x′∣x)[log⁡q(x′∣x)−log⁡p(x′∣x)]\sum_{x'} q(x'\mid x)[\log q(x'\mid x) - \log p(x'\mid x)]∑x′​q(x′∣x)[logq(x′∣x)−logp(x′∣x)] where the sum is over neighboring states. This provides a local training signal analogous to denoising score matching but for discrete spaces. It could be combined with the CTMC framework above to train discrete diffusion samplers without path-space divergences.

Concrete / Gumbel-Softmax relaxation. Relax discrete variables to continuous ones using the Gumbel-Softmax trick, apply continuous diffusion, then discretize at the end. This allows using the full continuous-time machinery (Langevin dynamics, path-space divergences) on problems that are fundamentally discrete. The tradeoff is that the relaxation introduces bias, and the quality of the continuous approximation degrades for highly structured discrete problems.

4. Conclusions and outlook

The central question of this post was whether diffusion models, originally designed for data-rich generative modeling, can be repurposed to sample from distributions specified only by a formula. The answer is a qualified yes. A useful theoretical framework now exists: the Schrödinger bridge / stochastic optimal control perspective connects continuous-time SDEs, discrete-time GFlowNet-style objectives, and classical methods like AIS under a shared language. The Radon-Nikodym derivative between forward and backward path measures is a common building block for many training objectives, and the asymptotic equivalences proved by Berner et al. [20]Berner, J., Richter, L., Sendera, M., Rector-Brooks, J., Malkin, N. (2026). From Discrete-Time Policies to Continuous-Time Diffusion Samplers: Asymptotic Equivalences and Faster Training. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2501.06148 show that discrete-time RL-style losses (TB, DB) can converge to continuous-time path-space counterparts as the time discretization is refined.

On the discrete side, the picture is younger but developing rapidly. GFlowNets provide a flexible framework for sequential construction of combinatorial objects, DiffUCO enables parallel non-autoregressive generation, and DASBS extends the Schrödinger bridge theory to discrete state spaces via the cyclic group trick. The structural parallels between continuous and discrete are striking: flow conservation mirrors the Fokker-Planck equation, detailed balance has the same form in both settings, and the same TB/LV/DB hierarchy of objectives applies.

That said, the practical gap between theory and application remains wide. Systematic benchmarking [2, 21]He, J., Du, Y., Vargas, F., Zhang, D., Padhy, S., OuYang, R., Gomes, C., Hernandez-Lobato, J. M. (2025). No Trick, No Treat: Pursuits and Challenges Towards Simulation-free Training of Neural Samplers. arXiv:2502.06685

Blessing, D., Jia, X., Esslinger, J., Vargas, F., Neumann, G. (2024). Beyond ELBOs: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Variational Methods for Sampling. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning PMLR, 235, 4205--4229. arXiv:2406.07423 reveals that neural samplers still struggle with mode collapse in high dimensions, that simulation-free training fails without Langevin preconditioning, and that classical Parallel Tempering MCMC combined with a post-hoc generative model can outperform the tested neural methods. The ELBO, the most common evaluation metric, is insensitive to missing modes, which means reported numbers can mask serious failures.

Several directions look promising for closing this gap.

Hybrid neural-classical methods. Rather than replacing MCMC, neural samplers may work best alongside it. Classical MCMC provides robust exploration (mode discovery), while neural networks provide amortized generation (fast sampling once trained). Injecting parallel tempering swaps or HMC leapfrog steps directly into neural SDE frameworks could combine the strengths of both.

Better parameterization and architecture. The Langevin preconditioning finding shows that how the target gradient ∇log⁡π\nabla \log \pi∇logπ enters the network matters more than the choice of loss function. Principled architectural choices that build in the right inductive biases are underexplored.

Improved discretization. Better SDE integrators (adaptive step sizes, higher-order methods, nonuniform time grids) could close the gap between continuous-time theory and discrete-time practice. Berner et al. [20]Berner, J., Richter, L., Sendera, M., Rector-Brooks, J., Malkin, N. (2026). From Discrete-Time Policies to Continuous-Time Diffusion Samplers: Asymptotic Equivalences and Faster Training. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2501.06148 show that training with coarse random discretizations and evaluating with fine grids already works surprisingly well.

Exploration techniques from RL. Mode collapse is fundamentally an exploration problem. Entropy bonuses, population-based training, curiosity-driven exploration, and off-policy replay buffers are all applicable and only partially explored in this setting.

Scaling discrete methods. DiffUCO and DASBS have been validated on standard benchmarks (Ising models, Max-Cut, Maximum Independent Set), but scaling to real-world combinatorial problems with heterogeneous constraints (protein design, logistics, scheduling) remains open. Progress in discrete diffusion for language modeling (masked diffusion, CTMC-based models, score entropy losses) has not yet been fully transferred to the sampling-from-energy setting.

Unifying continuous and discrete. The structural parallels between continuous SB/SOC and discrete SB/SOC, together with the asymptotic links between GFlowNet objectives and neural SDE objectives, hint at a broader framework that has not yet been fully written down. DASBS [43]Guo, W., Zhu, Y., Du, X., Nam, J., Chen, Y., Gomez-Bombarelli, R., Liu, G., Tao, M., Choi, J. (2026). Discrete Adjoint Schrodinger Bridge Sampler. arXiv:2602.08243 makes this connection more concrete, but a unified theory covering arbitrary state spaces, reference processes, and objective hierarchies remains elusive.

Training-free methods. DPSMC (§2.5) shows that classical SMC can be effective within the diffusion path framework without any learned parameters. Exploring training-free analogs for discrete spaces, and understanding when learning helps versus when classical estimation suffices, is an important open question.

The field is moving fast. The theoretical foundations are increasingly solid, the connections between communities (MCMC, variational inference, diffusion models, GFlowNets, optimal control) are becoming clearer, and the practical tools are improving. The most impactful advances will likely come not from any single method but from combining ideas across these traditions.
